items.title: AWS Updates Lambda Timeout and Adds GPU Support
items.summary: AWS announced updates to its Lambda service, including doubling the timeout from 30 minutes to 60 minutes, and introducing support for running on GPUs.
items.articleBody: AWS has expanded the timeout limit for its Lambda service, increasing the maximum execution time from 30 minutes to 60 minutes. This change is significant for developers who previously had to manage their code to run within a 30-minute window. The update comes after years of maintaining a 15-minute timeout limit, which was last adjusted in 2018. This new limit is expected to allow for more complex and resource-intensive tasks to be handled efficiently within the service. Additionally, AWS Lambda now supports running on GPUs, providing a new level of processing power for applications that require high-performance computing capabilities. This addition to the service is expected to benefit developers working on applications such as machine learning, data processing, and other compute-intensive tasks.

items.title: NVIDIA Launches Holiday Campaign Encouraging Play, Build, and Create with Technologies
items.summary: NVIDIA, the technology company, is promoting a holiday campaign encouraging users to engage in various creative activities using their technologies. The campaign aims to inspire people to explore new hobbies or improve existing ones.
items.articleBody: The holiday season is traditionally a time for giving, but NVIDIA is encouraging recipients to give themselves something to look forward to. The company is launching a campaign that promotes the use of its technologies for play, building, and creating. This campaign is designed to inspire users to explore new hobbies or enhance existing ones. One of the key points of the campaign is the promotion of new games, which are expected to be released in the coming months. These games are expected to offer a new level of engagement and enjoyment for players. NVIDIA is also highlighting the versatility of its technologies, such as its graphics processing units (GPUs), which can be used in various applications including gaming, design, and education. The campaign aims to show how these technologies can be used to create and share content, making the holiday season more engaging and interactive.

items.title: Why AI Agents Cost More Than Chatbots—and What It Means for Users
items.summary: AI agents can handle multi-step tasks, but a single request can trigger many model calls, searches and tool uses behind the scenes. This explainer covers what drives those costs and what to check before paying for an agent service.
items.articleBody:
AI agents promise to do more than answer questions. They can research topics, use software tools, compare information, and work through tasks involving several steps. But that extra capability introduces an important question: how much does it cost to complete the work?

The answer depends on how an agent operates. A task that looks simple on your screen may involve repeated AI requests, online searches, code execution, and other computing resources behind the scenes.

For users and businesses, understanding these costs helps explain why the value of an AI agent depends on more than its monthly subscription price.

What makes an AI agent different?

A basic chatbot interaction might involve asking a question and receiving an answer. An agent can go further by deciding which steps to take, calling tools, checking results, and continuing until it reaches an outcome.

For example, an agent researching a purchase might search several websites, compare specifications, investigate conflicting information, and prepare a recommendation.

That is an illustrative workflow, not a guarantee that every agent can perform those actions reliably. The important distinction is that one user request can trigger many operations.

Why the computing costs add up

Google Cloud's documentation identifies several factors involved in estimating agent costs: model tokens, agent behaviour, and supporting infrastructure.

Tokens are the pieces of text or other information a model processes. An agent may consume additional tokens each time it receives instructions, reads tool results, or generates its next action.

Costs can also include the services surrounding the model, such as search, computing resources, session storage, and monitoring. A longer or more complicated workflow can therefore require more resources than a short conversation.

This means that counting user messages alone is not enough to understand how expensive an agent is to run. What happens between the request and the final answer matters.

What Anthropic's research shows

In a published engineering report, Anthropic described the resource demands of its research-agent systems. In the company's data, agent interactions typically consumed about four times as many tokens as chat interactions, while multi-agent systems consumed about 15 times as many.

Those figures describe Anthropic's observations in that setting. They are not universal benchmarks, and they do not mean every agent costs four or 15 times more in money. Actual spending depends on model prices, tools, and implementation.

The findings nevertheless illustrate a practical trade-off: assigning more AI work to a task can improve results, but it can also increase resource consumption.

What users should check before paying

The company operating an agent pays for its underlying resources, but the customer's bill depends on the product's pricing terms. Before subscribing, check the following.

Included usage: How many tasks, credits, or requests does the plan cover?

Limits: What happens when you reach the allowance?

Extra charges: Are additional usage or connected services billed separately?

Task suitability: Can the agent handle the work you actually need?

Review effort: How much checking and correction will its output require?

Avoid assuming that access to an agent means unlimited work. Read the current plan details and test it with a representative task.

Measure the cost of a useful result

A practical way to judge an agent is to compare its cost with the value of work it completes successfully.

Consider a hypothetical task that usually takes you an hour. If an agent produces a usable result and you need only ten minutes to review it, the time saved may justify the price. If you spend the same hour correcting its mistakes, the benefit is much smaller.

For a small website owner, that makes a limited trial sensible. Start with one repeatable task, track the results, and record both the subscription expense and your review time.

AI agents can be useful without being suitable for every job. Before paying for more capacity, establish whether the tool consistently saves you time on the work that matters.

Sources:

Anthropic: How we built our multi-agent research system
https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system

Google Cloud: Estimate your monthly costs
https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/estimate-costs

items.title: Amazon has a plan to index the world’s online shopping data
items.summary: Amazon is reportedly building a project called World Product Graph, which would gather data on almost every product sold anywhere in the world, including items Amazon does not stock. According to a Reuters exclusive, the aim is to keep shoppers on Amazon.com and give AI shopping agents a reason to start their searches there. Amazon disputes the report's figures on its own assistant, saying they are outdated.
items.articleBody:
Amazon is reportedly working on an internal project that would turn its website into the main reference point for product information across the internet. According to an exclusive Reuters report published on November 13, the initiative is called World Product Graph. Its aim is to collect and organise data on almost every item sold anywhere in the world, including products Amazon does not stock itself.

Reuters says it based its report on an internal Amazon planning document, known as a PR/FAQ, and on people familiar with the matter. The central idea is simple: if Amazon holds the most complete and accurate catalogue of product details, shoppers have less reason to leave Amazon.com to compare options, check specifications or read about alternatives on other sites.

Why Amazon wants this now

The timing reflects a shift in how people shop online. Search engines such as Google have long been the starting point for product research, and rivals such as Walmart have been growing their e-commerce businesses. A new threat has also appeared in the form of AI shopping agents, which are assistants that search, compare and sometimes buy on a person's behalf. Reports on the plan name Meta's Muse and Perplexity among the tools Amazon is watching.

An agent that works for the shopper has no loyalty to any single store. Reuters reports that the people it spoke to see the product graph as a way to give those agents a reason to come to Amazon. If the best data on every product is on Amazon.com, an agent looking for answers is more likely to start there than at a competitor.

The problem with Amazon's own assistant

The report also says the document points to weaknesses in Amazon's own AI shopping tool. That tool launched as Rufus and, since May, has been marketed as "Alexa for Shopping." According to the report, the planning document acknowledged that the assistant sometimes gave inaccurate information, and a broader, cleaner product database was seen as a way to fix that.

Amazon disputes the picture. In a statement to Reuters, the company said the usage figures in the document are "significantly outdated." It also said its own data shows Alexa for Shopping is roughly 97% accurate worldwide.

Not the first attempt

The idea builds on earlier work. In 2025 it was reported that Amazon was developing a project called Starfish, which aimed to simplify how third-party sellers create product listings and to improve the quality of its catalogue data. World Product Graph appears to take that ambition much further. It would cover the whole market rather than only items listed on Amazon.

What is still unknown

Much remains unclear. The reporting rests on an internal planning document, and plans of this kind can change or be dropped before launch. It is not known when, or whether, World Product Graph will go live, and nothing is confirmed about how the data would be collected from other retailers. Nor is it clear how sellers, competing stores and regulators would respond to a company holding data on products it does not sell.

Why it matters

If the plan succeeds, it could strengthen Amazon's position as the default place to research and buy products, and it could pull traffic away from search engines and rival retailers. For shoppers, it could mean more consistent and detailed product information in one place. It would also add to the data and influence of a company that already dominates online retail. Competitors, sellers and AI developers will be watching closely to see whether Amazon moves ahead with it.

items.title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
items.summary: As companies let AI agents pull data from many systems at once, security teams are finding that guarding apps, networks and devices is not enough. A sponsored MIT Technology Review report, produced with security firm Cyberhaven, argues that organisations also need data lineage: a record of where data came from, how it changed and where it went.
items.articleBody:
As businesses hand more everyday work to AI agents, a basic security question is getting harder to answer: where did the data in an agent's output actually come from? A sponsored report published by MIT Technology Review on November 4, 2026, produced with the data security company Cyberhaven, argues that the answer depends on a concept called data lineage.

Consider a simple example. A sales representative asks an AI agent for a customer's pricing. To respond, the agent may draw on several places at once: a restricted pricing system, internal messages and old archived quotes. The answer can look perfectly reasonable, yet it may combine information that was never meant to be mixed or shared with that person. Nobody reviewing the result can easily tell which source contributed what.

Why traditional security falls short

Most security tools were built around specific things: applications, systems, networks or individual devices. The report's central argument is that this approach is no longer enough when software agents act on behalf of employees and move information between many of those places at machine speed. Securing agents at scale, it says, requires understanding how data moves, and not only where it sits.

What data lineage means

Data lineage is a record of a piece of data's life: where it originated, how it moved, how it was changed and where it ended up. For human workers, security teams have long relied on this kind of trail in some form. The report says teams now need it across human, agent-driven and mixed workflows so that governance, accountability and trust can be maintained.

Industry analysts who follow the topic describe a related problem, sometimes called an agentic data lineage gap. Security teams can often see that an agent took an action, but not where its data came from, how it was transformed or where it was sent next. Without that context, an alert is harder to investigate and a policy is harder to enforce.

The wider framework

Cyberhaven's own guidance groups agent security into three pillars: visibility into what agents are doing, identity for the agents themselves, and guardrails that limit their behaviour. It describes data lineage as the link that connects the three. It also argues that fixed, rules-based guardrails tend to be brittle when agent behaviour changes quickly.

A vendor with a product to sell

Readers should keep in mind that the report is sponsored content and that Cyberhaven sells products in this area. The company launched an AI-native data security platform called Flow on July 28, 2026, and added an Agentic Data Security module to it in early November. The argument that lineage is essential is also the argument for buying such a tool. That does not make it wrong, but it should be weighed alongside independent research and other vendors' approaches.

What is still unknown

The report makes a case, but it does not settle how much lineage tracking organisations actually need, how well it works across different tools and agents, or what it costs in complexity and privacy. It is also unclear how quickly companies will adopt such controls compared with how quickly they are deploying agents.

Why it matters

Agents are being given access to more company data, and in many organisations the controls have not kept pace. Any company that lets agents handle customer, financial or internal information will need to be able to show where that information came from and where it went. Data lineage is one of the leading proposals for doing that, and the debate over how to implement it is only beginning.

items.title: Critical Rails Flaw Lets Attackers Write Server Files via Crafted ImageMagick Uploads
items.summary: Rails has patched a critical flaw in its Active Storage upload component that could let an unauthenticated attacker write files to a server by uploading a specially crafted file, if the app processes uploads with ImageMagick. Fixed versions 8.0.5.2 and 8.1.4.1 were released on November 4, and teams are urged to upgrade and review their image-processing settings.
items.articleBody:
The Ruby on Rails team has fixed a critical security flaw in Active Storage, the framework component that handles file uploads. According to the project's advisory, published on November 4, 2026, an unauthenticated attacker could write arbitrary files to a server by uploading a specially crafted file, provided the application processes uploads with ImageMagick. The Rails advisory is tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 and carries a severity score of 9.8 out of 10.

How the flaw works

ImageMagick decides how to read a file based on its contents rather than its file name. Some of its internal format handlers, known as coders, do more than decode a picture. They can follow instructions inside the file that touch other files on the server. Reports on the advisory say Active Storage did not restrict any of these coders, and its image analyzer runs as soon as a file is attached. That means a crafted upload does not need a preview or a resized version to be requested before it can cause harm.

Applications that use the Disk storage service face an additional risk. The advisory says the same path can also allow arbitrary files readable by the application to be read, which could expose secrets and credentials.

Who is affected

Security analysts summarising the advisory say an application is exposed when three conditions are met. It uses Active Storage with ImageMagick for image processing, it accepts uploads from untrusted users, and its ImageMagick security policy does not already block the affected coders. One report notes that the default policies packaged by Debian and Ubuntu do not block them.

The affected versions of the activestorage package are those older than 8.0.5.2 and the 8.1 line before 8.1.4.1. Applications on other branches should check the official advisory for guidance.

What to do

The Rails team released the fixes in versions 8.0.5.2 and 8.1.4.1 on November 4. Teams running affected applications should upgrade as soon as possible. Where an immediate upgrade is not possible, the advisory describes a workaround that involves tightening ImageMagick's security policy so the risky coders are blocked.

For apps that use the Disk service, the maintainers advise rotating secret_key_base and any other secrets the application process could read, since those may have been exposed if the flaw was abused. Security writers also recommend reviewing upload activity and looking for unexpected file changes on servers that met the conditions above.

A familiar pattern

The incident is another reminder that image-processing tools do more than open pictures. Coverage of the Rails flaw points to earlier problems involving ImageMagick in other products, including a WordPress issue and a Discourse image pipeline attack, where the tool was pushed into reading or acting on files it should not touch. The common lesson is that uploads from untrusted users need strict limits on what the software handling them is allowed to do.

What is still unknown

Reports differ on the identifier. Some outlets say no CVE number had been assigned when the advisory was published, while another cites CVE-2026-66066, so readers should check the official advisory for the current status. None of the coverage reviewed said the flaw was being exploited in the wild, and the vulnerability had not been listed in CISA's known-exploited catalogue at the time one analyst wrote about it. That could change.

Why it matters

Rails runs a large number of online stores, software-as-a-service products and startup apps, and many of them accept file uploads from the public. A flaw that needs no login and can lead to file writes and secret exposure is one that attackers tend to look at quickly. Any organisation running Rails with ImageMagick should confirm its version, apply the update and rotate secrets where the advisory calls for it.

items.title: Xen Hypervisor Flaws Let One Malicious VM Read and Write Any Other VM's Memory
items.summary: The Xen Project has disclosed two flaws, tracked as XSA-523, that let a malicious virtual machine read and change the memory of other VMs on the same host, including the privileged control domain known as dom0. Patches are available, but there is no workaround, so operators of Xen-based servers need to update the hypervisor and restart the host.
items.articleBody:
Two serious flaws in the Xen hypervisor can let a malicious virtual machine break out of its isolation and read or change the memory of other virtual machines on the same physical server. The Xen Project disclosed the problems on November 3, 2026, in security advisory XSA-523, which covers two vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704. The advisory's impact statement says a malicious guest can read and write arbitrary memory belonging to other domains, including dom0.

What dom0 is and why it matters

Xen runs ordinary workloads in guest virtual machines, while a special privileged virtual machine called dom0 manages everything else on the host. By default, dom0 has full permissions. If a guest can write into dom0's memory, the separation between tenants on that server effectively disappears. Vates, the company behind XCP-ng, describes the risk as a single compromised guest being able to take over the whole host.

How the flaws work

Xen lets one virtual machine grant another access to specific pages of its memory, and the hypervisor checks permissions so that each VM only touches what it has been granted. According to coverage of the advisory, the flaws sit in the code that handles grant copy operations. To save time when copying a batch of data within the same memory page, Xen reuses permission checks it has already made. In some cases it failed to check again when it should have, which let a guest reach memory it had no right to access.

An attacker who exploits this could read other tenants' data, keys and secrets held in memory, and write into other domains. Security researchers who examined the issue say Xen versions from 4.6 onward are affected.

Who is affected

Multi-tenant servers, where several customers' virtual machines share one host, carry the highest risk. That includes cloud and hosting providers as well as organisations that run Xen-based platforms. Vendors built on Xen, including XCP-ng, Citrix XenServer and Qubes OS, have published their own update guidance. Qubes, for example, has a fixed Xen package for Qubes 4.3 that is rolling out in stages and requires a restart of dom0 afterwards.

What to do

The advisory reports no known workaround, so the only real fix is a patched hypervisor from the Xen Project or from the platform vendor. A new hypervisor only takes effect after the host is restarted, so operators need to plan maintenance windows. Anyone who builds Xen from source should read the instructions for their release carefully, because the patches may depend on other code changes that are missing from the downloaded files. At least one security analysis also notes that older Xen releases may have no upstream patch available, which leaves those deployments reliant on vendor support or an upgrade.

What is still unknown

No attacks using these flaws had been reported at the time of the coverage reviewed. It is also not yet clear how many older or self-managed deployments will be left unpatched, or how quickly hosting providers will complete the required restarts.

Why it matters

Hypervisor isolation is the foundation of virtualisation security. Customers who share hardware rely on it to keep their data separate, and a guest-to-host escape undermines that promise. The flaws are a reminder that even mature, widely reviewed software can hide serious mistakes in its most sensitive code. Organisations that run Xen directly, or buy hosting from providers that do, should check their patch status and ask whether affected hosts have been updated and restarted.

items.title: Radio With No Radar: Why Agent Runtime Security Fails Without the Layers Beneath It
items.summary: Many AI agent security products promise to stop harmful actions in real time, but a security-vendor analysis argues that promise only holds when an agent's traffic passes through a gateway the company controls, which most agents never do. The piece says runtime enforcement needs a clear picture of what agents can reach and what is normal for them, or it is working blind.
items.articleBody:
Nearly every pitch for AI agent security now ends with the same promise: the product will stop the bad action in real time. A recent analysis published by The Hacker News on November 4, 2026, which appears to come from the security vendor Reco, argues that this promise is only true for a narrow kind of agent. It holds for agents whose traffic passes through a gateway the company owns. Most agents, the author says, never touch one.

Where agents actually run

The argument starts from a practical observation. Many of the agents employees use today live inside platforms and applications the company does not fully control, such as business software, assistants and tools built into services. In that setting the application itself is the runtime. A security team cannot simply place an inspection point in front of the agent, because the agent's activity never travels through a path the company owns.

The article illustrates the risk with an everyday case. An employee approves an action without realising the assistant is about to bypass the sanctioned system, and an unknown number of external recipients end up receiving email from a personal account instead of the approved channel. Nothing in that sequence looks dramatic, which is why it is hard to catch.

Radio without radar

The headline's metaphor sums up the thesis. The author compares runtime enforcement to an air-traffic controller who has a radio but no radar. The controller can issue commands with authority, but without knowing which plane is where and where it is headed, every instruction is a guess delivered confidently.

In this picture, runtime enforcement is the radio. The radar is what the article calls posture: what an agent is able to reach, what counts as normal behaviour for it and whom it is acting on behalf of. The article says runtime controls only work well when that underlying picture exists.

Why context decides whether controls work

Without context, security teams face a familiar trade-off. If a tool blocks too much, the business finds ways to route around it. If it blocks too little, it becomes little more than a logging system that adds delay. The article's conclusion is that useful runtime security must stop the genuinely harmful action without stalling the many legitimate actions around it, and that takes knowledge of identity, permissions and normal behaviour.

The argument rests on three points: agents run inside platforms, individual components of those platforms can themselves be targets, and good decisions need context. Together these suggest that runtime protection is the last step in a chain of controls rather than a replacement for the earlier ones.

Others make a similar point

Other security writers have reached related conclusions. Analysts who focus on non-human identities argue that runtime detection often sees behaviour only after an identity boundary has already been crossed, and that an agent holding a broad access token can do real damage before an alert arrives. Their advice is to start with identity and permission design and use detection to confirm the limits are holding.

A vendor's perspective

Readers should remember that this analysis comes from a company that sells products in the layers it says are neglected. The argument can be right and still serve a commercial purpose. It should be weighed against independent research and against the claims of runtime-security vendors, who would say that real-time enforcement is necessary even if it is not sufficient.

What is still unknown

The article is an opinion and framing piece and not a measurement. It does not establish how many enterprise agents operate outside company-owned gateways, how often runtime tools fail for lack of context, or how much the layered approach it recommends would cost or reduce risk in practice.

Why it matters

Companies are adopting agents faster than they are building the controls around them. A tool that promises to block bad actions in real time can create false confidence if the security team cannot see what the agent can access or what it normally does. The practical lesson is to check that agent security rests on visibility and permissions first, and to treat real-time blocking as one layer rather than the whole defence.

items.title: China-Aligned Hackers Hijack Sogou Input Method DNS Requests to Deploy DarkVigil Backdoor
items.summary: Researchers at ESET say a China-aligned group called SlippyNunchucks hijacked internet lookups made by the Windows version of Sogou Input Method, a popular Chinese-language typing tool, to install a spying backdoor called DarkVigil. Tencent fixed the weakness in version 16.10, and users are urged to update.
items.articleBody:
A China-aligned hacking group has turned a popular Chinese-language typing program into a delivery route for spyware, according to research published by the security firm ESET on November 4, 2026. The group, which ESET calls SlippyNunchucks, abused the way the Windows version of Sogou Input Method fetched part of its settings, and used it to install a backdoor known as DarkVigil. Sogou Input Method is a widely used input method editor developed by Tencent.

How the attack worked

ESET says a component of Sogou Input Method requested a "brand-promotion" configuration from a Sogou server over plain, unencrypted HTTP. Because that traffic was not protected, the attackers could use DNS hijacking, a technique that quietly redirects a program's lookup to a different server, to send those requests to infrastructure they controlled. That server returned a malicious configuration instead of the real one.

The altered configuration then led a legitimate Sogou component to download files that included a signed program and a booby-trapped library of the same name that it loaded. This method, known as DLL side-loading, makes the malicious code run under the cover of a trusted program. The end result was the DarkVigil implant running on the victim's computer.

What DarkVigil is

DarkVigil, also known as FDMTP, is a modular toolset written in .NET with more than 20 plugins. ESET has tracked the malware and its operator since early 2025. The activity was described as part of a surveillance campaign, which points to espionage rather than ordinary financial crime.

Timeline and victims

ESET says the Sogou activity began on July 1, 2026, and that victims were spread across six countries. The activity followed an earlier supply-chain compromise involving the software QuickFox. The researchers saw the group switch to Sogou three days after QuickFox released a clean version. Other applications mentioned as having been abused by the same actor include QingTalk, MiYunChat, SoftCam and tawk.to.

The number and spread of victims first made the researchers suspect a software exploit, but the investigation traced the problem to the insecure connection instead.

The fix

Tencent addressed the issue in Sogou Input Method version 16.10, released on October 30, 2026. According to security summaries of the research, the update moves the affected requests from HTTP to HTTPS and adds certificate validation, which prevents a redirected server from impersonating the real one. Users should update to version 16.10 or later. Security teams are advised to watch for unexpected files named after Adobe software inside Sogou's components folder and for unusual network connections from the app. ESET's report contains the full technical indicators.

Not the first Sogou problem

This is not the first time Sogou Input Method has been used this way. In September 2026, Gen Digital reported that a separate, now-patched flaw in the software was exploited by another China-linked group to deliver a different backdoor.

What is still unknown

ESET has not established where the DNS hijacking took place. The researchers say possibilities include compromised routers with altered DNS settings, routers carrying a DNS-hijacking implant, or interception at the level of an internet provider. It is also unclear how many people were ultimately infected, who the specific targets were, and whether the group has other delivery routes ready.

Why it matters

The case shows how a harmless-looking background request, such as one for a small image or settings file, can become an attack path when it is not encrypted. Because the traffic looked like normal application behaviour, victims had little chance of noticing. Users and organisations with Sogou Input Method installed should update it, check their router and DNS settings, and treat any software that still uses plain HTTP for updates or configuration as a risk.

items.title: Apple Music's upcoming feature will let you record yourself doing karaoke
items.summary: Apple Music is adding a karaoke video feature called Selfie Sing, which lets iPhone users film themselves with the front camera while singing along to on-screen lyrics, then save or share the clip. The feature was spotted in the first iOS 27.3 developer beta, with a public release expected in December.
items.articleBody:
Apple Music is preparing a new karaoke-style feature called Selfie Sing that lets people record videos of themselves singing without leaving the app. The feature appeared in the first developer beta of iOS 27.3, which Apple released on November 3, 2026, and a public release is expected in December.

What Selfie Sing does

With Selfie Sing, an iPhone user can sing along to a song while the front-facing camera records them, with the lyrics shown on screen. According to the description shown in the feature, users can adjust the vocal effects on their voice, then save the video or share the performance with friends. Until now, anyone who wanted to make a singing video would typically have to switch to another app to film it.

The feature builds on Apple Music Sing, the karaoke mode that Apple introduced in late 2022 with iOS 16.2. That tool lets listeners reduce the original singer's vocals and follow animated lyrics. Selfie Sing adds the camera on top of it.

Who found it and how to try it

The feature was first spotted by Aaron Perris in iOS 27.3 beta 1. Beta users can find it by searching Apple Music for a playlist named Selfie Sing. Tech sites report that the playlist is visible even on iPhones running iOS 27.2, but the option to turn on the camera and record only appears on the iOS 27.3 beta.

Early limits

The feature is clearly still in testing. Coverage of early hands-on use says only a small number of songs support it so far, with one report counting six. It also appears to be limited to iPhones. AppleInsider reported that the camera option did not show up on an iPad Pro running the iPadOS 27.3 beta. Aaron Perris's demonstration video used an Animoji in place of his face, but reports say Selfie Sing does not support Animoji yet.

Other changes in the beta

Selfie Sing is not the only Apple Music change in this beta. 9to5Mac reports that iOS 27.3 also improves the lyrics view when the phone is held in landscape orientation.

What is still unknown

Beta features can change or be removed before release, so the final version of Selfie Sing may look different. It is not yet clear how many songs will be supported at launch, whether it will come to the iPad or other devices, what the sharing options will be, or whether it will be available in every region where Apple Music operates. Apple has not published detailed information about the feature in the coverage reviewed.

Why it matters

Short singing videos are a popular form of content on social platforms, and music services have been looking for ways to give listeners more to do than press play. By adding recording and sharing directly to Apple Music, Apple is making its app a place where people can create content as well as listen. If Selfie Sing launches broadly in December, it could also give Apple Music subscribers a reason to spend more time in the app and put it in competition with the karaoke and video features of other music and social apps.

items.title: Binance attackers used fake job interviews to pull off $6.3 billion crypto heist
items.summary: Binance says the record $6.3 billion theft from the exchange began months earlier, when attackers used fake job interviews and tampered software to compromise the computers of its engineers. The FBI has reportedly blamed North Korea, while Binance's account shows how social engineering can open the door even at the world's largest crypto exchange.
items.articleBody:
Binance has shared more details about the cyberattack that cost it roughly $6.3 billion in digital assets, the largest crypto theft on record. The exchange said on November 3, 2026, that the attackers did not break in through a single technical flaw. Instead, they spent months preparing, using fake job interviews and tampered software to take over the computers of its own engineers.

How the attack began

According to Binance's account, as reported by several outlets, the attackers used a bogus job interview and malicious software hidden in an advertisement to compromise the computers of two software engineers. They then used a third engineer's computer to drain the funds. One report says the chain started in June, when a member of Binance's wallet developer team downloaded an AI tool that had been tampered with.

The details point to a patient operation. A fake recruitment process gives an attacker a believable reason to contact an engineer, ask them to run code or install software, and gain access to a device that may hold sensitive credentials. In this case the targets were developers who worked close to the systems that move customer funds.

Who is blamed

Engadget reports that the FBI says North Korea was behind the attack. Axios similarly reports that North Korea appears to have used a fake job interview as part of its months-long preparations. Another outlet links the activity to a North Korean group known as TraderTraitor, a name previously associated with attacks on crypto companies that used fake job offers. Binance's own statement, as summarised in these reports, focused on the methods used rather than on naming a culprit, so the attribution should be treated as reported rather than as a final finding.

How long it lasted

One report says the thieves were still moving crypto out of the exchange nearly four hours after the first theft. That detail suggests the attackers had access that could not be shut off immediately, although the full timeline of Binance's response has not been set out in the coverage reviewed.

Who is affected

Binance has not been described in these reports as passing the losses on to customers in the coverage reviewed here, and it is important to check the exchange's own updates on this point. The incident is nonetheless a serious event for the whole crypto industry, because Binance is the world's largest exchange and the theft is far larger than previous record heists.

Why the method matters

The case is a warning that the weakest point in a company's security is often a person's workstation rather than the exchange's core systems. Even a firm with advanced defences can be breached if an employee runs a malicious file during what looks like a job application. It also shows how attackers are turning to trusted tools, including AI tools, and to advertisements as ways to distribute malware.

Security experts commonly advise companies to keep developer machines separate from systems that can move funds, to require approval from more than one person for large transfers, and to train staff to treat unsolicited job offers and tests with caution. Individuals applying for jobs should be wary of any recruiter who asks them to download software or run code on a work device.

What is still unknown

Many questions remain. Binance has not publicly detailed how much of the stolen crypto can be recovered or frozen, and law enforcement has not said how the funds were laundered. It is also unclear exactly how the attackers moved from three compromised computers to the systems that held the assets, and whether other firms were targeted using the same approach.

Why it matters

A theft of this size shakes confidence in the safety of crypto exchanges and is likely to bring more scrutiny from regulators and law enforcement. It also reinforces the concern that state-backed hackers are using crypto theft to raise money. For companies of every size, the lesson is that a convincing recruiter message can be as dangerous as a software vulnerability.

items.title: Valve just changed its Steam release rules amid a flood of AI games
items.summary: Valve has tightened Steam's release process after approval times for new games stretched to as long as 12 business days. Developers must now run their game through Steam for at least five minutes before submitting it for review. Valve's announcement does not mention AI, but developers blame a surge of AI-made games for the backlog.
items.articleBody:
Valve has changed the rules for releasing games on Steam in an attempt to clear a growing backlog of approvals. The update, announced to Steamworks developers in early November 2026, comes as review times for new games have stretched to as long as 12 business days. Valve's own target is three to five days, according to coverage of the delays.

What is changing

The headline change is simple. Developers must now run their game through Steam for a minimum of five minutes to confirm that it works on the platform before they submit it for review. The new release checklist asks for more checks up front, and it targets builds that are broken or incomplete. A build is the packaged version of a game that a developer sends to Valve for testing and distribution.

Valve says a large part of the backlog comes from re-reviewing games that failed these basic checks the first time. Each failed submission has to go back into the queue, which slows down approvals for everyone else.

The AI question

Valve's announcement does not mention artificial intelligence. Even so, the timing has drawn attention. Developers and several news outlets link the delays to a flood of new titles, many of them made with AI tools, that reach review without the kind of testing a human-led project would usually have done. Engadget notes that this point is left unsaid by Valve, and one developer quoted in the coverage says the waiting time seemed to spike around September and October.

It is important to separate the claims. Valve has not said how much of the backlog is caused by AI-made games, and at least one report points out that the company has not measured AI's contribution at all. The new checklist is aimed at broken builds in general, whether a person or an AI tool created them.

Why this matters to developers

The delays are already causing problems. Indie developers report missing planned launch dates, in some cases by weeks. For a small studio, a release date is often tied to marketing, press coverage, a festival or a sale event, so a delay of that length can cost real sales. Studios that depend on a tight launch window have little room to absorb a longer review.

Background on Steam and AI

Valve changed its policy on AI-generated content in early 2024, after first rejecting some submissions. It said then that it would allow the vast majority of games that use AI, as long as developers disclose it and describe the guardrails they have in place to avoid illegal content. That policy made it easier for AI-assisted games to reach the store. The current backlog suggests the storefront is feeling the effects of that openness together with a general rise in submissions.

What is still unknown

Several questions remain. Valve has not said whether the five-minute rule will bring review times back to its three-to-five-day target, or how quickly. It has not published figures on how many submissions are AI-made or how many are failing basic checks. It is also unclear whether the company will add further measures, such as stronger automated checks or changes to AI disclosure.

Why it matters

Steam is the largest PC game store, and its review process decides when a game can reach players. A slow queue hurts honest developers most, while a flood of low-effort submissions can make it harder for players to find good games. The change is a modest one, but it shows that even a platform with a lenient AI policy has to adjust when volume goes up faster than its checks can handle.

items.title: Google Issues Patches for Critical Android Flaw That Could Allow RCE Without User Interaction
items.summary: Google's November 2026 Android security bulletin fixes a critical flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-58868, that could let an attacker run code on a phone remotely with no action from the user. It affects Android 14 through 17. Google says phones with a security patch level of 2026-11-01 or later include the fix, and no attacks have been reported so far.
items.articleBody:
Google has patched a critical Android vulnerability that could let an attacker run code on a phone remotely without the owner doing anything. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-58868 and is listed in the company's November 2026 Android Security Bulletin, which was published on November 2. It affects Android versions 14 through 17.

What the flaw is

Google rates CVE-2026-58868 as Critical and places it in the Android Framework, a core part of the operating system. The public description says it is a memory-safety error, specifically an out-of-bounds write caused by a heap buffer overflow in a piece of code that handles frame decoding. Flaws of this kind can allow a program to overwrite memory it should not touch, which is a common route to running attacker-controlled code.

Security reports describe it as a zero-click flaw, meaning a victim would not need to tap a link or open a file. However, neither Google's bulletin nor the public CVE record explains how an attacker would actually reach the vulnerable code, so the practical risk is hard to judge for now.

The wider update

The flaw is part of a large monthly release. The November bulletin lists 216 vulnerabilities, of which 23 are rated Critical and 193 High. Two other Critical flaws could also allow remote code execution, CVE-2026-58876 and CVE-2026-58936, and both sit in the System component. The bulletin additionally lists critical privilege-escalation issues, including CVE-2026-55275, which affects Android 16 and later.

Which patch level you need

Google splits its November fixes across two security patch levels. Devices with a patch level of 2026-11-01 or later include the fixes for the Framework, System and Android runtime components, which covers CVE-2026-58868. A patch level of 2026-11-05 or later covers every issue in the bulletin. The split lets phone makers ship the fixes common to all Android devices sooner.

Some analysts note that CVE-2026-58868 is not one of the fixes delivered through Google Play system updates. That means users should check the Android security update date on their phone and not rely only on the Google Play system update date.

How to check your phone

On most phones, you can find the patch level under Settings, then About phone, then Android version, where a line shows the Android security update date. If it shows November 1, 2026 or a later date, the fix is in place. If it shows an earlier date, check for a system update. Phone makers and carriers release patches on their own schedules, so some models will get the fix later than others.

Is it being exploited?

Reports based on Google's bulletin say that no exploitation has been reported, and one analysis notes that the flaw is not listed in the US government's catalogue of known exploited vulnerabilities. That could change if attackers reverse-engineer the fix, which is a common pattern after a patch is released. Google's bulletin gives no workaround for phones that cannot install the update.

The bigger problem: phones that never get updated

One news outlet reports that nearly half of active Android devices will never receive this patch, because they run older versions or come from makers that no longer provide updates. That figure is that outlet's claim and should be treated with some caution, but the underlying issue is well known. Flaws in newer versions of Android are fixed on paper, while many older or unsupported phones stay exposed.

What is still unknown

Technical details are limited. It is unclear what kind of content or message could trigger the flaw, whether it can be exploited reliably, and how long it will take manufacturers to roll out the fix across their ranges. Researchers may publish more detail as they study the patch.

Why it matters

A flaw that can run code with no user action is among the most serious kinds of bug on a phone, because it removes the usual advice to avoid suspicious links. Anyone with a phone on Android 14 to 17 should check for the November update and install it as soon as it appears. Organisations that manage fleets of Android devices should confirm patch levels across their devices and plan to replace phones that can no longer be updated.

items.title: CISA Confirms Hackers Exploiting WordPress Core Flaw During Software Upgrades
items.summary: CISA has confirmed that attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-119977, a WordPress Core flaw that can let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a server while a full-package core upgrade is in progress. WordPress released patches on October 28, and CISA added the bug to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 3.
items.articleBody:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has confirmed that attackers are actively exploiting a flaw in WordPress Core, the software that powers a large share of the world's websites. The agency added the vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-119977, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 3, 2026, about six days after WordPress shipped a fix.

What the flaw is

CISA describes the bug as a time-of-check to time-of-use race condition. It affects the way WordPress carries out full-package core upgrades. According to the agency's alert, the problem is caused by predictable, web-accessible staging paths used while the upgrade is running. During that short window, an unauthenticated attacker, meaning someone with no account on the site, can execute code on the server.

Security reports rate the flaw at 8.1 on the CVSS scale and say it affects WordPress versions from 4.7 through 7.1.3. Importantly, the weakness is in WordPress itself and not in a third-party plugin or theme, so a site is not safe just because it uses well-maintained add-ons.

Timeline

WordPress released patches on October 28, 2026. Details of the flaw emerged shortly afterwards when the security firm Wordfence published its analysis and noted that exploitation does not need a login. CISA added the flaw to the KEV catalog on November 3. By the time of The Hacker News report on November 4, Wordfence said it had blocked 12,632 attempts to exploit the flaw. Reports say CISA gave US federal agencies a short deadline of November 6 to remediate.

Why the upgrade window is the risk

The vulnerability only matters while a core upgrade is under way, because that is when the staging files exist. Analysts note that repeated requests can help attackers catch the short window, although such requests alone do not prove a site was breached. This is what makes the bug unusual. The act of updating, normally the safe thing to do, is the moment of exposure.

Even installing the fix may not be risk-free. In a follow-up on November 6, The Hacker News reported research from Umut Bayram of Picus Security, who found that some sites can still be attacked while they install the fix for this flaw. The first update to the fixed release, in other words, can leave some sites exposed one last time.

What site owners should do

WordPress administrators should update to the patched release for their branch as soon as possible and confirm the version through their dashboard or the official WordPress site. Because of the finding about the first update, sites that are exposed to the internet during an upgrade should consider when and how they run it. Administrators should also look for signs of compromise, such as unexpected files, unfamiliar administrator accounts or odd entries in server logs around upgrade times. Hosting providers that run upgrades for customers should check how their process handles the window.

A pattern of core flaws

This is not the first WordPress Core flaw to appear in the KEV catalog this year. Several other Core vulnerabilities, including an SQL injection issue in July and a remote file inclusion issue in September, have been listed for active exploitation. That does not mean WordPress is uniquely weak, but it does show that attackers are watching the core software closely and acting quickly after patches appear.

What is still unknown

It is not clear how many sites have been compromised, who is behind the attacks, or what attackers are doing once they gain access. The reports also do not say how many sites are still running vulnerable versions. The list of exact fixed versions for each branch should be checked against the official WordPress announcement.

Why it matters

WordPress runs a vast number of business, news and e-commerce sites, and many of them update automatically or through shared hosting. A flaw that can be used without a login, that is already being exploited, and that is tied to the update process itself leaves little time to react. Site owners should treat this as an urgent update and check their sites carefully afterwards.

items.title: AMD rides data center riches to ‘largest and most profitable’ quarter in history
items.summary: AMD posted record third-quarter revenue of $13.4 billion, up 45% from a year earlier, driven by a 97% jump in data center sales to $8.5 billion. The chipmaker forecast about $17 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter, well above what analysts had expected, though its gaming business shrank and cash flow weakened.
items.articleBody:
AMD has reported the biggest quarter in its history, with demand for artificial intelligence hardware pushing its data center business to nearly double in a year. The chipmaker released its third-quarter 2026 results on November 3, covering the period that ended September 26. CEO Lisa Su described the quarter on the earnings call as the largest and most profitable in the company's history.

The headline numbers

Revenue came in at $13.4 billion, up 45% from $9.2 billion a year earlier and up 16% from the previous quarter. That was above the top of AMD's own forecast range of $12.7 billion to $13.3 billion, and above the roughly $13.1 billion that analysts had expected, according to figures cited by Shacknews and The Next Web.

Profit rose even faster than sales. On a GAAP basis, net income was $2.4 billion, or $1.46 per diluted share, up from $0.75 a year ago. Excluding items such as stock-based compensation, earnings per share were $2.09, up 74%. Gross margin was 54% on a GAAP basis and 56% on a non-GAAP basis.

Data center drives the results

The data center segment generated $8.5 billion in revenue, up 97% from $4.3 billion a year earlier. It now accounts for about 64% of AMD's total revenue, compared with 47% a year ago. Operating income in the segment reached about $2.9 billion, up from $1.1 billion. AMD credited strong demand for its EPYC server processors and the launch of its Instinct MI450 series of AI accelerator chips.

Other parts of the business did less well. Client and Gaming revenue fell 8% to $3.7 billion. Within that segment, sales of client processors rose 7% to about $2.95 billion on demand for Ryzen laptop chips, while gaming revenue dropped 40% to $773 million because of lower sales of custom chips and graphics products. Embedded revenue grew 29% to $1.1 billion.

What AMD expects next

AMD guided for fourth-quarter revenue of about $17 billion. That implies growth of roughly 66% from a year earlier and about 27% from the third quarter, and it is above the $16.2 billion that analysts had forecast. Su said she expects growth to accelerate as AMD scales up production of its Helios rack-scale systems and its next-generation Venice server processors. She also told analysts she expects revenue to grow by more than 80% in 2027, with data center as the largest contributor.

Shares rose more than 5% in after-hours trading following the report.

Where the cautions are

The strong income statement was not matched by cash flow. Reports on the results say free cash flow fell by almost two-thirds, with inventory building and capital spending weighing on cash conversion. That is common for a company ramping up production of complex new products, but it is something investors will watch.

There is also a concentration risk. With data center sales supplying nearly two-thirds of revenue, AMD's fortunes are tied closely to how long the AI infrastructure spending boom continues at its current pace. The company's gaming business, once a main pillar, is shrinking.

What is still unknown

The guidance is AMD's own forecast and not a result, and it depends on the new products reaching volume production on schedule. It is not yet clear how the company's margins will develop as the Instinct and Helios systems scale, or how much of the demand comes from a small number of very large AI customers.

Why it matters

AMD is the main challenger to Nvidia in AI chips, and these results show it winning a growing share of the money companies are spending on AI data centers. For the wider industry, the numbers are another sign that demand for AI computing capacity remains strong, even after a recent period of nervousness in chip stocks. For AMD, the next few quarters will test whether it can turn rapid revenue growth into steady profits and cash.

items.title: iPad mini OLED vs. iPad mini: What's new?
items.summary: Apple's new OLED iPad mini, announced on October 26, changes much more than the screen. It also brings the A20 Pro chip, a thinner body, newer wireless chips, an IP67 water-resistance rating and a rearranged front camera. The starting price is $699, which is $100 above the current iPad mini 7.
items.articleBody:
Apple's new iPad mini, announced on October 26, 2026, is being described as the OLED iPad mini, and the display is the headline change. But comparisons with the 2024 iPad mini 7 show that the update reaches well beyond the screen, with a new chip, a thinner body, upgraded wireless hardware and water resistance. It also costs more.

The display

The new model has an 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR OLED screen, replacing the 8.3-inch Liquid Retina LCD on the iPad mini 7. OLED panels light each pixel individually, which gives deeper blacks and stronger contrast, especially in dark video scenes. The new screen is also brighter, reaching up to 1,200 nits of peak brightness when showing HDR content. One thing has not changed. Reports on the specifications say the screen still lacks ProMotion, Apple's high-refresh-rate feature found on its Pro iPads.

Design

The new iPad mini is thinner, at 5.4 mm compared with 6.3 mm for the iPad mini 7, and it is slightly narrower. Its dimensions are listed as 195.3 by 132.6 by 5.4 mm, against 195.4 by 134.8 by 6.3 mm for the older model. It also gains an IP67 rating, which means it is protected against dust and temporary immersion in water. Both models keep a USB-C port, and neither works with Apple's Magic Keyboard.

Performance

Inside is the A20 Pro chip, replacing the A17 Pro in the iPad mini 7. Apple says it delivers up to 1.6 times the CPU performance and up to 2.7 times the graphics performance of the A17 Pro generation. These are the company's own best-case claims. According to one comparison, the 128GB and 256GB models use a 5-core CPU, while the 512GB model gets a stronger chip configuration, which matters for buyers who want the most performance.

Connectivity and audio

The tablet uses Apple's in-house N1 wireless chip, which brings Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support. The iPad mini 7 supports Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3. Cellular models move to Apple's C2 modem, which Apple says can deliver up to 50% faster cellular data speeds with better power efficiency. Engadget also notes a new speaker arrangement that Apple calls Acoustic Display.

Cameras and charging

The front camera is now a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera placed on the landscape edge with an f/2.0 aperture. On the iPad mini 7, the 12-megapixel camera sits on the portrait edge and has an f/2.4 lens. The placement makes video calls feel more natural when the tablet is held horizontally. Apple also advertises faster charging, but one comparison points out that this needs a suitable adapter, and the 20W adapter included in the US is below the stated requirement.

Price

The extra hardware comes with a higher cost. In the US the new model starts at $699 for 128GB with Wi-Fi, with 256GB and 512GB versions at $799 and $999. The 128GB cellular model costs $849. The iPad mini 7 launched in 2024 at $499, but Apple raised its price to $599 in June 2026, citing rising memory and storage costs. That makes the OLED model a $100 step up from the current iPad mini 7 price, and a $200 increase over the original launch price. Cult of Mac argues that the OLED screen alone justifies a $100 premium over the older model but calls $699 an expensive tablet.

Who should upgrade

People who read, watch video or play games on their iPad mini and want a better screen, a lighter device or stronger performance for demanding apps will see the largest gains. Those who mainly need a basic compact tablet may be better served by the cheaper iPad mini 7, which is still sold. Buyers coming from older mini models will notice the biggest jump.

What is still unknown

The comparisons published so far rely on Apple's specifications and claims. Independent testing of battery life, sustained performance, screen quality and real-world cellular speed will show how much of the promised gains reach everyday use. It is also unclear how long the iPad mini 7 will remain on sale at its new price.

Why it matters

The iPad mini is a niche product that Apple updates only every few years, so each new version tends to bring a big change at once. Moving to OLED fits Apple's wider shift toward the technology across its products, and it narrows the gap between the mini and the Pro iPads. The higher prices, however, show how component costs are affecting Apple's lineup.

items.title: Your phone's apps could have more permissions than they need – here's how to check
items.summary: Many smartphone apps ask for access to your camera, microphone, location or contacts, and not all of them need it. A quick review in your phone's settings can show which apps hold which permissions and let you switch off the ones that are unnecessary.
items.articleBody:
Most smartphone apps need some permissions to work. A maps app needs your location, and a camera app needs your camera. But apps are often given more access than they really need, usually because we tapped "Allow" when we first opened them. A short review of your settings can show what each app can reach and let you take back anything that is not necessary.

Why it matters

Permissions let apps see data such as your location, photos, contacts and microphone. In the best case, an app uses that access only for the feature you want. In the worst case, a poorly built or malicious app can collect information it does not need, share it with advertisers or expose it to criminals. Security guides also note that cutting back on permissions can help battery life, because fewer apps work in the background.

A simple rule is to ask whether an app really needs a given permission to do its job. The more sensitive the data, the stronger the reason for access should be. A photo editor needs your photos, but a simple game that asks for your contacts or microphone deserves suspicion.

How to check on Android

Menu names vary slightly between phone makers and Android versions, but the steps are similar on most devices.

Open Settings and look for a section named Privacy or Security and privacy, then choose Permission manager. This shows a list of permission types such as Camera, Microphone, Location and Contacts. Tap any one of them to see which apps can use it, and change an app's setting to deny it.

You can also work app by app. Go to Settings, then Apps, choose an app and tap Permissions to see everything it can access. For location, Android usually offers more than on or off. You can allow access all the time, only while the app is in use, or not at all. For most apps, "only while using" is a sensible choice.

Many recent Android versions also include a privacy dashboard that shows which apps have recently used the camera, microphone or location, which helps you spot an app that is using access more than you expect.

How to check on iPhone

On an iPhone, open Settings and go to Privacy and Security. You will see a list of data types, including Location Services, Contacts, Photos, Camera and Microphone. Tap any of them to see which apps have asked for access and switch individual apps off.

You can also open Settings, find the app in the list and review the permissions that appear there. For location, iPhone lets you choose options such as never, ask next time, or only while using the app.

Engadget also points to the App Privacy Report on iPhone. When it is turned on, it shows which apps have accessed your data and sensors, and it lists the network domains apps contact and when. That makes it useful for spotting an app that behaves in an unexpected way.

What to look for

Focus first on the most sensitive permissions: location, microphone, camera, contacts and photos. Look for apps that have access they plainly do not need, such as a flashlight, wallpaper or simple game asking for your contacts or microphone. Check for apps that have background location access when they only need it occasionally.

Next, remove access you do not need. If an app stops working properly after you turn off a permission, you can switch it back on. If you no longer use an app, uninstalling it removes its access completely. It also helps to read reviews and check the developer before installing a new app, and to approve only the permissions that are essential.

Make it a habit

Review your permissions every few months, and again after installing several new apps or after a major system update, since updates can add new privacy controls.

What is still unknown

How much each individual app actually does with its permissions is often unclear, since apps do not always explain how they use data. The settings described here show what an app is allowed to do, not what it has done, which is why the privacy dashboard on Android and the App Privacy Report on iPhone are useful additions.

Why it matters

Your phone holds your location history, photos, messages and contacts. Regular permission checks are one of the easiest ways to limit how much of that information leaves your control, and they take only a few minutes.

items.title: Your desktop's front USB ports may be slowing down every device you plug into them
items.summary: Front USB ports on a desktop PC are convenient, but they can deliver less speed and power than the ports on the back. Because they connect to the motherboard through extra internal cabling, and are sometimes built to an older standard, they can slow down file copies and phone charging.
items.articleBody:
The USB ports on the front of a desktop computer are easy to reach, but they are not always as good as the ones on the back. Depending on the device you plug in, you may see slower file transfers, slower phone charging or in some cases a device that does not work properly. A guide published by Engadget on November 4, 2026, explains why this happens and how to avoid it.

Why front ports can be slower

The ports on the back of a desktop are usually attached directly to the motherboard, so data and power travel a short path. Front ports sit on the case and connect to the motherboard's internal connectors through extension cables, which makes the path longer. Engadget notes that this is a matter of how the machine is built and not a fault with your computer.

Other factors can add to the difference. Front ports are sometimes tied to older connector standards inside the machine. Writers on the subject note that front ports on some desktops are only USB 2.0, which tops out at 480 Mbps in theory, while the rear ports are faster USB 3.x ports. Cable quality inside the case also matters. One technical guide explains that a case with a basic USB 3.0 cable connected to a faster header can end up limited to 5 Gbps. Another consideration is sharing. Several front ports may run through the same controller, so devices on them can compete for bandwidth.

It is not a universal rule

Engadget stresses that this is not true of every machine. Some modern PCs have high-end ports on the front. Apple's latest Mac Studio is an example from the other direction. The base model has two 10 Gbps USB-C ports on the front, but its Thunderbolt ports are only on the back, so the front ports are useful but slower.

What it means in practice

For everyday accessories, the difference is small. A mouse, keyboard or headphones use little power and need little bandwidth, so they work fine on front ports. The problem shows up with devices that need speed or power. An external SSD or flash drive may copy files noticeably more slowly. One tech site gives the example of a flash drive that normally reaches 80 to 150 MB/s but might lose around half of that on a front USB 2.0 port. Phones may charge more slowly, and devices such as webcams or high-speed storage may behave badly or fail on a slow port.

How to tell which port is which

Check the port itself. Colour coding can help, although manufacturers do not follow it strictly. Black ports are typically USB 2.0, blue ports are usually USB 3.0 and teal ports are intended for USB 3.1 Gen 1 or faster. Symbols such as "SS" next to a port also point to higher-speed standards. The most reliable method is to look up your motherboard or computer model and read the specifications for each port.

You can also run a simple test. Copy a large file to the same drive while it is plugged into a front port, then do it again with the drive on a rear port. If the rear port is much faster, the front port is the bottleneck. If a front port does not reach the speeds you expect, swapping the case's internal cable to a different motherboard header may help, although this depends on what the board and case support.

What to plug in where

A sensible approach is to keep the rear ports for external drives, fast flash drives, VR headsets, cameras and anything that needs full power or speed. The front ports are better for occasional use, such as headphones, a mouse or keyboard, or a quick charge. If you use a USB hub, connect it to the best port you have, because everything plugged into a hub shares the same bandwidth.

One thing that is not affected is the speed of your computer's internal storage. Games and programs load from the internal drive, which does not use the front USB ports at all.

What is still unknown

The exact speeds depend on your particular case, motherboard and cables, and manufacturers do not always make the differences clear. The reports also say it is easy to overlook how much a port affects results until you test it.

Why it matters

Many people assume every USB port on a computer is the same. Knowing that they are not can save time on large transfers and avoid confusing problems with devices that seem slow or unreliable. A few seconds spent choosing the right port is often the cheapest upgrade available.

items.title: Please stop asking me when the AI bubble will pop
items.summary: Nobody can say when, or even whether, the AI market will have its crash, and a growing number of analysts argue that the question itself is the wrong one to focus on. This explainer looks at why bubbles are so hard to time, what experts say could trigger a pop, and what readers can usefully watch instead.
items.articleBody:
"When will the AI bubble pop?" has become one of the most common questions in technology and finance. A first-person column published by The Verge on November 3, 2026, captured the mood. Its author said people keep asking, with a mix of excitement and nervousness, and replied that anyone who truly knew would be making a huge bet on the market rather than answering questions. The joke makes a serious point. Even people who are convinced a bubble exists have a hard time saying when it will end.

Why timing is so hard

Economist Dean Baker, writing in September 2026, argued that you cannot mark the date of a burst on a calendar. He noted that it is hard to know what bursts a bubble, even after the fact. The 2008 housing crash is sometimes described as predictable because the reset dates on risky loans were known in advance, but Baker was sceptical that a similar schedule exists for AI spending.

A Harvard Business Review article from September 2026 describes a parlor game in company boardrooms, in which executives ask whether there is an AI spending bubble and when it will pop. Its authors argue that the more useful question for business leaders is how to operate in this environment, not when the market will turn.

What people say could trigger a downturn

Observers point to a few possible pressure points. Investor Ray Dalio has said that rising debt levels and elevated interest rates could prove too much for a hot market. Other commentators point to the huge amounts being spent on data centres compared with the revenue AI products currently bring in. A recent SiliconANGLE report argues that Nvidia's recent partnerships, which turn AI computing power into collateral for financing, tie parts of the system together, so that a slowdown in demand would spread through it.

Markets have already shown nerves. Commentary in early November referred to an AI-focused sell-off, and coverage of AMD's results noted that chip stocks had a rough week beforehand. AMD then reported record revenue, which shows that company results and market sentiment do not always move together.

The case against a single big pop

Not everyone expects a dramatic crash. Some analysts argue that AI is several markets moving at different speeds, including chips, cloud services, models and applications, so stress may show up in one layer long before another. One blogger predicted that a bubble, if there is one, may shrink slowly when a more attractive trend appears, and not burst suddenly. A CFA Institute blog post published on November 4 reports that its author set out to prove that AI was a bubble, and came away more bullish after examining the evidence, while saying he would turn more cautious if data on rental prices, usage and contract cancellations deteriorated.

Why it matters beyond investors

An NPR piece in October raised a different worry: that a burst could cause a recession, which in turn could speed up the replacement of workers with AI. Whether or not that comes to pass, the point is that the effects of a bust would reach well beyond technology shares.

What to watch instead

Rather than trying to guess a date, analysts suggest tracking measurable signs. These include whether customers keep using and paying for AI products, whether the cost of renting computing power holds up, whether companies cancel or delay data centre contracts, and how much of the spending is funded with debt. Company earnings, such as AMD's latest results, add useful information, but a strong quarter does not settle the larger question.

What is still unknown

Experts do not agree on whether AI is in a bubble at all, let alone on the timing. Much of the evidence is open to different readings. High spending can be a sign of excess or of strong demand, and only time and results will show which.

Why it matters

The AI boom affects stock markets, pension funds, jobs and the plans of nearly every large company. A clear, honest answer to the timing question is not available, and a confident prediction should be treated with caution. This article is general information and not investment advice.
