items.title: Arkane and its Blade game may end up at Ubisoft as Xbox considers offers
items.summary: Bloomberg reports that Ubisoft and at least two other companies have offered to buy Arkane, the studio behind Dishonored and Deathloop, from Xbox. Xbox has not agreed a deal with any buyer, and a sale could decide whether Marvel's Blade, the studio's long-awaited next game, gets finished.
items.articleBody:
Xbox is reportedly weighing offers to sell Arkane, the studio behind Dishonored and Deathloop, and the French publisher Ubisoft is said to be among the bidders. According to a Bloomberg report by Jason Schreier published on November 3, 2026, Ubisoft and at least two other gaming companies have made offers. The other bidders have not been named. The report cites people familiar with the matter, and Xbox has not agreed a deal with any buyer.

The sale is tied to the future of Marvel's Blade, the action game Arkane has been developing since it was announced in 2023. Reports say a sale would most likely let the studio finish the game, which Bloomberg's sources expect to be released within the next year or two.

Background: Xbox's restructuring

The potential sale follows a major reorganisation at Xbox under CEO Asha Sharma. In July, Xbox announced about 1,600 immediate job cuts, with roughly 3,200 more planned over the 2027 fiscal year. Xbox said at the time that none of its publicly announced first-party games would be cancelled as part of the reductions. Arkane has been part of the Xbox family since Microsoft bought Bethesda's parent company in 2021. Arkane's sister studio in Austin, Texas, closed in 2024 after the game Redfall failed.

Earlier reports raised the possibility that Xbox might close the Lyon studio altogether, which would have put Blade at risk. Bloomberg's Schreier has said he would be surprised if the studio were shut down, and a sale is described as an alternative to closure.

The options on the table

Besides outside buyers, reports say Xbox has also considered selling the studio to its own management. That would leave Arkane independent, probably with outside financing. The terms of the offers have not been disclosed, and it is not known whether Microsoft has a preferred buyer.

Some outlets report that a French newspaper put the number of jobs at risk at around 217 if no buyer emerges, but Xbox has not confirmed that figure. One report also says Xbox has until December 13, 2026, to strike a deal, but this rests on a single outlet and has not been confirmed by the companies.

Labour tension

The situation has caused friction at the studio. Video Games Chronicle reported that the union representing Arkane workers has accused Xbox of "sabotaging" the development of Blade. Xbox has not responded to that claim in the coverage reviewed.

What is still unknown

Several important questions remain. Neither Microsoft, Xbox, Ubisoft nor Arkane had commented publicly on the report at the time of writing. The identities of the other bidders are not known, and nor is how much any of the offers are worth. It is also unclear whether the rights to Marvel's Blade would transfer with the studio, who would publish the game, and whether Marvel would need to approve a change of ownership. A release date has not been announced.

Why it matters

For players, the main question is whether Marvel's Blade survives and where it ends up. A sale to a publisher with its own plans could change how and when the game is released. For the industry, the story is another sign of how Xbox is reshaping its portfolio, selling or spinning off studios it no longer wants to run directly. It also marks a possible turnaround for Ubisoft, which has been facing its own pressures but is now reported to be looking to add a well-regarded studio.

For Arkane's staff, the outcome will decide whether the studio keeps its jobs, its identity and its projects. The coming weeks should show whether Xbox picks a buyer, a management buyout or another route.

items.title: What made Nothing's CMF Phone 2 Pro so much cheaper than others?
items.summary: Nothing's CMF Phone 2 Pro launched at $279 by keeping a big screen and battery while cutting costs elsewhere. It uses a cheaper MediaTek chip, electronic rather than optical image stabilisation, a single speaker, slower 33W charging and a lower water-resistance rating than the pricier Nothing Phone 3a.
items.articleBody:
When Nothing's budget sister brand CMF launched the Phone 2 Pro, the most common reaction was surprise at how little it cost. The phone started at $279 in the US beta programme, with UK prices of £219 for the 8GB RAM and 128GB model and £249 for the 256GB version. A recent Engadget explainer, published on November 3, 2026, looks at how CMF managed it. The short answer is that the company kept the features most buyers notice every day and made trade-offs in areas that are easier to overlook.

What CMF kept

The Phone 2 Pro has a large 6.77-inch AMOLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate, and a big battery that Nothing says can last close to two days on a charge. It also has a three-camera setup that includes a telephoto lens, a feature normally found on more expensive phones. Engadget says CMF kept the big screen and battery but made compromises elsewhere.

Where the savings came from

Engadget compares the phone with the pricier Nothing Phone 3a and finds several differences.

The processor is one of them. The CMF Phone 2 Pro uses MediaTek's Dimensity 7300 Pro chip, while the Phone 3a uses Qualcomm's Snapdragon 7s Gen 3. The two are notably different processors, and the CMF's chip is a lightly improved version of the one in the original CMF Phone 1.

The cameras are another. The main and telephoto cameras on the Phone 2 Pro rely on electronic image stabilisation rather than optical image stabilisation, which uses a physical mechanism in the lens. The Phone 3a's main camera has true optical stabilisation. That means the cheaper phone can take decent photos, but it may struggle in shaky hands or poor light.

There are also less glamorous cuts. The Phone 2 Pro has a single speaker. Its charging speed tops out at 33W, compared with 50W on the Phone 3a. It has an IP54 rating for dust and splash resistance, below the Phone 3a's IP64. BGR adds that CMF used a plastic back panel and frame instead of the glass and metal found on pricier models. Reviewers also note there is no wireless charging and no charger in the box.

Engadget concludes that none of these compromises feel like dealbreakers, and together they explain a lot of the price gap.

The limits of the explanation

Nothing has not published a part-by-part bill of materials for the phone, so it is impossible to say exactly how much each decision saved. The explanations in the coverage are informed comparisons and not a breakdown from the company.

A different pricing climate

The story also carries a warning about the present. Commentary from T3 suggests that the same trick may be harder to repeat, because the components a successor would need are no longer cheap. Apple recently raised the price of its older iPad mini, citing rising memory and storage costs, which shows that component prices are now pushing prices up across the industry. If those costs stay high, a phone like the CMF Phone 2 Pro may be harder to build at such a low price in the future.

What to take from it

For buyers, the lesson is to look at what a cheap phone leaves out and to decide whether those omissions matter to you. If you care most about screen size, battery life and general performance, the CMF approach delivers. If you take a lot of low-light photos, want stereo sound or need strong water resistance, a more expensive phone may be worth the extra money.

What is still unknown

Prices and availability differ by country, and the US beta programme limits who can buy CMF phones. Long-term software support and durability are also open questions for a budget phone.

Why it matters

The CMF Phone 2 Pro shows that a phone can feel good to use without a premium price when a company chooses its trade-offs carefully. It also shows how quickly that kind of value can disappear when component costs change.

items.title: NVIDIA's controversial DLSS 5 is coming to RTX Remix to 'enhance' older games
items.summary: NVIDIA is adding its controversial DLSS 5 technology to RTX Remix, its free tool for modding older PC games, so modders can apply AI-driven lighting and detail to classic titles. Reviewers are split on how it looks, it can be costly on frame rates, and it often fails with games that use anti-cheat software.
items.articleBody:
NVIDIA is bringing DLSS 5, its most controversial graphics technology yet, to RTX Remix, the free modding platform for older PC games. According to Engadget, the support arrived on October 23, and it gives modders a way to apply DLSS 5 to classic titles that never had it. The move is likely to renew an argument about whether AI should decide how games look.

What RTX Remix is

RTX Remix has been available for free since early 2024. It lets modders add ray tracing and AI-upscaled textures to older games, effectively remastering them with modern graphics. Adding DLSS 5 extends that toolkit to a technology that goes much further than ordinary upscaling.

Why DLSS 5 is controversial

Earlier versions of DLSS mainly made games run faster or look sharper by reconstructing images at higher resolutions. DLSS 5 is different. NVIDIA presented it at its GTC 2026 event as a form of neural rendering that adds realistic lighting and detail. Early demonstrations drew sharp criticism. Some commentators compared the effect to an AI beauty filter that changes how game characters look, and the phrase "AI slop filter" spread quickly on social media. TechSpot noted that its more realistic skin textures might not suit games with a stylised art direction, such as Final Fantasy VII Rebirth. Critics also pointed to cases where faces appeared to age, which could contradict a character's story.

NVIDIA says developers keep artistic control over how the technology is applied. DLSS 5 officially launched on September 3 with NBA 2K27, initially limited to the newest RTX 50 series graphics cards, and later reached a second game, Hogwarts Legacy, on November 5, in a more restrained form.

How it works in older games

Modders had access to DLSS 5 files after they leaked from an early build of NBA 2K27, and community tools such as DLSS 5 Manager and DLSS 5 Swapper now let users add it to many Vulkan and DirectX games on NVIDIA RTX cards. With the Remix update, the process becomes part of a supported modding platform.

Engadget's tester says that in four games they tried, they preferred the overall look with DLSS 5 turned on, and they recommend enabling it mainly in games where you regularly see your character's face. Another writer argues the better question is whether a particular game and mod actually work well, since "enhance older games" sounds broader than the evidence supports. Older games were designed within limits. Flat lighting, for example, can be an artistic choice, such as a dark corridor in a horror game that hides an enemy, and not just a technical limit.

The costs and caveats

DLSS 5 is demanding. Unlike earlier DLSS versions, which were designed to raise frame rates, it can cut performance by 50% or more in some games, according to one summary, so it needs a powerful PC. Engadget's tester did report performance improvements in several games after installing the update through an NVIDIA app beta driver, so results appear to vary.

The larger obstacle is anti-cheat software. DLSS 5 mods generally do not work well with games that use it. Reports give GTA V Enhanced as an example of a game that may fail to launch. Engadget's writer expects the problem to ease once NVIDIA officially supports DLSS 5 in more titles, but that has not happened yet.

What is still unknown

It is not clear how widely modders will adopt DLSS 5 in Remix projects, how well it will run on cards other than the RTX 50 series, or whether NVIDIA will add tools that let modders limit or tune its effect on faces and skin. The long-term view of players may also change. Even some developers who criticised the technology at first have said they warmed to it.

Why it matters

Remix already lets fans modernise games that are decades old. Adding DLSS 5 raises the stakes, because it shifts part of a game's look from artists to an AI model. Whether players see that as a welcome upgrade or an unwelcome filter will decide how far the technology spreads.

items.title: Here's how to adjust Apple AirPods for small ears
items.summary: People with small ears can often get a better AirPods fit by adjusting how the earbuds sit, trying smaller ear tips on AirPods Pro, running Apple's built-in fit test, or using foam tips. Standard AirPods without tips offer fewer options, so some users may be better off with a Pro model.
items.articleBody:
AirPods are among the most popular wireless earbuds, but they do not fit every ear equally well. People with small ears or narrow ear canals often find that the earbuds feel loose, fall out or fail to block outside noise. An Engadget guide published in November 2026 explains how to improve the fit, and the right approach depends on which AirPods you own.

If you have standard AirPods without ear tips

Standard AirPods have no tips, so your options are limited. The main method is to push the earbud gently into your ear and rotate the stem toward your face until it locks in place. Engadget notes that people with small ear canals may find it hard to get the tight fit they need. If that applies to you, regular AirPods might not be the best choice, and some users get a better result by moving to AirPods Pro.

If you have AirPods Pro

AirPods Pro come with silicone ear tips in several sizes, which gives you much more room to adjust. The number of sizes depends on the generation. The first-generation AirPods Pro include small, medium and large tips. The second generation adds an extra-small size. The AirPods Pro 3 go further and include an extra-extra-small tip, which can help people with particularly small ear canals. The tips attached when you first open the box are medium.

Choosing the right size is not always obvious. A smaller tip is not automatically the best choice for a small ear, so it is worth trying every size in the box.

Run Apple's fit test

Apple has a built-in test that checks whether your tips create a good seal. Put the AirPods Pro in your ears, open Settings on your iPhone, choose your AirPods and tap the ear tip test. It is called Ear Tip Fit Test or Test Acoustic Seal, depending on the model. Tap Continue and then Play. You will hear a short piece of music, and the result will tell you whether you have a Good Seal or whether you should adjust the buds or try a different size.

If the result is poor, reposition the earbuds, try the test again, and then switch to another tip size and repeat it. Some guides suggest tilting the buds so they sit more vertically in your ears. You can also play bass-heavy music as a quick check. A good seal makes the bass sound fuller.

Changing the tips

Swapping tips takes only a few moments. You pull the old tip off and press the new one onto the earbud until it clicks into place. Follow Apple's instructions for your specific model, since the connector changed on the AirPods Pro 3. Accessories made for earlier models may not fit correctly, and tips from the first-generation AirPods Pro are not designed to be interchanged with the second generation, according to Apple.

Consider foam tips

Some people with small or unusually shaped ear canals find foam tips more comfortable and secure. Foam is soft and pliable, and it is typically squeezed before you put it in your ear so that it expands to fit. Apple introduced foam-infused tips with the AirPods Pro 3, but Engadget says pure foam tips may still work better for some people. Third-party tips can be a good option, but check that they are made for your exact AirPods model, and be cautious about unmarked listings.

When to consider a different model

If you have tried every size and still cannot get a secure fit, the problem may be the design and not the tips. Engadget says some users may achieve a better fit by upgrading to AirPods Pro. For people with the smallest ear canals, the extra-extra-small tips on the AirPods Pro 3 may help, though this is not guaranteed.

What is still unknown

Fit is personal, and there is no exact science to it. What works for one person may not work for another, and tip availability and test names vary by model and software version.

Why it matters

A poor fit affects more than comfort. Earbuds that do not seal properly lose bass, let in more noise and make noise cancellation less effective. Spending a few minutes on the fit can noticeably improve how your AirPods sound.

items.title: Meta's Quest 2 and Quest Pro reach 'end of feature development'
items.summary: Meta says its Quest 2 and Quest Pro headsets will get their final feature update by March 2027, ending new software features for the two devices. Security patches will continue through the end of 2027, and Meta says the app store, owned games and cross-play with newer Quest headsets will keep working.
items.articleBody:
Meta has told developers that its Quest 2 and Quest Pro virtual reality headsets have reached the end of feature development. The company published the announcement on its developer blog on November 2, 2026. It does not switch the headsets off, but it does mark the start of their wind-down.

The timeline

According to Meta's post and coverage of it, the final operating system update for both headsets is Horizon OS version 2.13, which is due to reach all Quest 2 and Quest Pro devices by March 2027. After that, the headsets will not get new system features. Meta says it will keep delivering security patches and critical bug fixes on a quarterly basis through the end of 2027. New app submissions for the two headsets will be accepted through December 2027.

What stays working

Much of Meta's message is about what will not change. Games and apps already bought will keep working, both solo and multiplayer, and the library stays available to download. The store will remain open on the headsets, and Meta says no app will be removed from it because of this change. Cross-play between the Quest 2, Quest Pro, Quest 3 and Quest 3S will continue to be supported. PC VR through Meta's Link feature, along with services such as avatars, voice calls and messaging, is listed among the features that keep working.

What changes for developers

Developers can keep releasing updates for existing apps, and Meta has not set an end date for that. However, the company says it will stop testing new operating system and SDK releases on the older headsets, so it will be up to each studio to make sure its apps work on them. Studios have several options. They can keep one version of a game for all devices, run separate builds, or freeze a final build for the older headsets and stop selling to Quest 2 and Quest Pro users. People who already own such an app keep it. Meta's app policy also requires developers to give at least 180 days' notice before ending support in a way that costs users content or essential services.

Why Meta is doing this

The Quest 2 has been on sale for about six years, and its mobile processor is now significantly outdated. That is the reason given for ending feature development. The timeline also follows Meta's treatment of the original Oculus Quest, which went through a similar sequence of ending features, then security fixes, then app updates.

What it means for owners

For people who only play the games they already own, nothing changes this winter. The main effect will be gradual. New system features will stop, and some new games and app updates that need newer software may skip the older headsets. One tech site notes that the date that matters most to an owner is the day the studio behind a favourite game decides to freeze its Quest 2 version, not a date Meta sets. Quest Pro owners are in the same position, with the same cutoffs, even though that headset cost a lot more at launch.

Those thinking about upgrading may want to consider the Quest 3 or Quest 3S, which Meta continues to support fully. Owners on a strict budget who mainly replay existing games have little urgency to switch.

What is still unknown

It is not clear how quickly major studios will stop supporting the older headsets, or how many new games will still ship for them in 2027. How well the older hardware copes without further system updates over a longer period is also an open question.

Why it matters

The Quest 2 helped bring consumer VR to a wide audience, and it is one of the best-selling headsets in the category. Its slow retirement shows how quickly VR hardware ages, and how much owners depend on the choices of Meta and game studios to keep their devices useful.

items.title: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity
items.summary: Anthropic has released FlashProve, an open-source research prototype that uses cryptographic proofs to show that an AI response was produced by a specific, publicly committed model, without exposing the model's private weights.
items.articleBody:
Anthropic has unveiled FlashProve, an open-source research prototype aimed at a problem most AI users never think about: when you send a prompt to an AI service, you have no technical way to confirm which model actually answered it. The announcement came in early November, and the code and technical documentation were published on Anthropic's GitHub repository.

FlashProve is built around an idea researchers call "provable inference." The AI provider first publishes a cryptographic fingerprint, known as a commitment, tied to the exact weights of a model. When the model later produces a response, a proof can be generated showing that the output came from the committed weights. Anyone can check that proof against the public fingerprint. The proofs rely on zkSNARKs, a type of zero-knowledge proof that confirms a computation was done correctly without revealing the secret numbers behind it. That matters because closed-model makers keep their weights private.

The researchers point to several uses. A provider could be stopped from quietly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a stronger model to inflate benchmark results. Third parties could also back up claims such as "this code was scanned by an advanced security model" or "this business plan was approved by a particular AI." Regulators could, in principle, check which models providers actually run. The verification step is designed to be light enough to run on a local device, so the customer does not need expensive GPUs.

Anthropic tested the system on Meta's Llama 4 Maverick, a 400-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model running with 4-bit quantized weights. According to The Decoder's reading of the technical report, proofs were generated at roughly 110 tokens per second on a single H100 GPU. Heise reports that an earlier open-source method, VerInf, needed about 14.3 hours for 1,000 tokens and produced a 93.6 GB proof. Anthropic also says its Claude model contributed key optimizations to the project.

The limits are significant. Anthropic stresses that FlashProve is a research prototype and describes it as unmaintained. Coverage also notes constraints around context window size, sampling and decoding support, and the high computing cost of generating proofs. Anthropic has said it has no plans to deploy FlashProve at its own services or at any other AI lab.

A verified identity would also say nothing about quality. Proving that a response came from a named model does not show that the answer is accurate, safe, or suited to a business task, and those still need separate evaluation.

Even so, FlashProve points toward a future in which model identity is checked alongside accuracy, safety and price, instead of being taken on the provider's word. Whether the industry adopts that idea will depend on whether proofs become cheap and fast enough to be routine.

items.title: Sonos adds new Presets and prepares for the 27voice AI beta
items.summary: Sonos has released an app update that finally lets listeners save one-tap Presets with a chosen room, music and volume, and it has opened a US-only early-access waitlist for 27voice, a cloud-based AI voice assistant, ahead of a wider launch planned for 2027.
items.articleBody:
Sonos has started rolling out a major app update that adds long-requested Presets and opens early access to its new AI voice assistant, Sonos 27voice. The update, reported as Sonos app 91.0, began reaching users on November 3.

Presets let you save a combination of music, room and volume, then start it with a single tap from the app's homescreen. Listeners have asked for something like this for years, and some reports describe it as the company's most-requested feature. One report says up to 50 Presets can be saved. There are limits for now. Presets can only be launched from the mobile app, and they do not work with voice commands or the Sonos web app. They also require S2 speakers running Sonos 27. Android support has been confirmed but is scheduled for a later update.

The bigger headline is Sonos 27voice, a voice assistant built on large language models and designed around music and home audio. Instead of rigid commands, it is meant to understand natural requests: starting music, moving playback between rooms, grouping or ungrouping speakers, and setting timers. Sonos says it can also handle more complex asks, such as finding an artist's newest album and playing it in a chosen room, or identifying an album from its cover art. It can also report the weather and control supported smart home accessories.

Access is limited. In the United States, eligible users can request a place on the waitlist from November 6 through Settings, General Settings, Voice Assistants in the Sonos app. Approved testers get access from November 12. The early-access phase is available only in the US and only in English, and Sonos plans a full release in 2027 after collecting feedback from the smaller group.

The update also brings smaller changes. A left swipe on the Now Playing screen or mini player now skips to the next track, favorites can be rearranged, and iPhone users get System Health, an iOS-only diagnostics view that helps spot network and speaker connection problems.

The main trade-off is privacy. Unlike Sonos's earlier Voice Control, which stays local, 27voice sends voice requests to Sonos's cloud servers. Reports also say some open-ended questions are handled with outside AI models, and that some data may be processed in the US or by outside AI companies. Sonos says the assistant is optional. Presets and System Health work without enabling it, and users can stay on Classic Voice Control. Sonos also says Alexa and 27voice can be active on the same compatible speaker.

For Sonos owners, Presets are an immediate, practical improvement, while 27voice is an early look at where the company's software is heading. What remains unclear is how well the assistant performs in everyday use, how Sonos will handle voice data, and when the beta will reach other countries and languages.

items.title: Data centers are turning to old jet engines as the wait for power grows
items.summary: With grid hookups and new gas turbines taking years to arrive, some AI data center builders are buying retired aircraft engines and converting them into on-site power generators. The approach is fast but less efficient and dirtier than conventional power plants.
items.articleBody:
Some AI data center developers are turning to a surprising source of electricity: retired jet engines. The New York Times reported on November 3 that builders stuck in long queues for grid connections and new turbines are installing converted aircraft engines to generate their own power on site.

The reason is time. According to the International Energy Agency, connecting even 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia takes about seven years. New gas turbines, meanwhile, are reported to take around six years to deliver in the United States, and a Mitsubishi Power executive has said most new capacity is expected to come online by 2031. Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen said that with jet-powered units, a data center can be running in about 24 months.

The engines are pulled from retired planes, often from desert storage yards, and rebuilt to burn natural gas. Companies such as ProEnergy and FTAI are in this business, reworking engine cores like those used on Boeing and Airbus jets into stationary generators. One report notes that an old engine can now be worth more as a power unit than as spare parts.

Elon Musk's xAI is among the companies already using them. The Times, citing state permits and satellite imagery, reported that xAI installed eight converted jet-engine turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center in Memphis. Separately, Crusoe walked away from a $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, which has started selling a version of its jet engine as a data center power plant. A Crusoe spokesperson said the company still plans to use turbines. Policy is adding pressure, since the Trump administration has been encouraging data centers to generate their own electricity.

The trade-offs are significant. Converted jet engines are less efficient and produce more pollution than turbines designed for conventional gas power plants, and operators need more of them to produce the same amount of electricity. Environmental groups such as the Southern Environmental Law Center are watching these projects, and some experts say efficiency and emissions concerns may carry more weight in a year or two. For that reason the engines are widely seen as a stopgap rather than a permanent solution.

The trend shows how far power supply has fallen behind the AI buildout. Companies that can afford to burn less efficient equipment may get online sooner than rivals waiting in line, but they also take on regulatory and reputational risk. Still unclear is how many of these units will be installed, how long they will stay in service, and whether faster grid connections or new turbine capacity will arrive in time to make them unnecessary.

items.title: Binance says hackers used fake job interviews and an internal AI tool to pull off the $6.3 billion heist
items.summary: Binance says the $6.3 billion theft, the largest in crypto history, was not a single exploit. In a postmortem, the exchange describes a months-long chain of attacks: a tampered AI coding tool, a fake recruitment interview, and an internal AI tool that let the attacker reach more engineers' machines.
items.articleBody:
Binance has published its account of how attackers stole an estimated $6.3 billion from the exchange in late October, the largest crypto theft on record. It surpasses the $1.5 billion taken from Bybit in February 2025. In a post on Tuesday, November 3, the company said the breach was not a single flaw but a chain of techniques that began months earlier and relied heavily on tricking people.

According to Binance, the preparation reaches back to June. A developer on its wallet team went looking for a popular AI coding tool, found it through a search engine, and installed it using a tampered Homebrew installation. Binance says it caught that first download, replaced the affected device and changed passwords. By then, though, the attackers had reportedly learned about the team's structure. Binance did not name the AI coding tool or the search engine involved.

In September, a second engineer who was job hunting went through what looked like a real hiring process, including a virtual meeting with the supposed CEO of a fictitious company. That interview led the engineer to download a malicious code repository. Binance has also said the recruiter built trust by sharing a social media account with personal photos and videos.

The decisive step came on October 20. Binance says the attacker used the compromised computer together with an internal AI tool to take control of the systems of two other wallet engineers. The company describes the overall attack as a combination of social engineering through fake recruitment, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise and an advanced method of authorizing transactions.

Binance says it has since rebuilt the affected wallet system in a new environment, tightened its internal AI tools and access controls, and put more money into AI-assisted threat detection. It also plans a security research fund and joint initiatives with leading AI companies. The company says it has replenished roughly 90 percent of the stolen assets, about $6 billion. Separately, Binance says it detected and blocked 57 suspected state-sponsored attack attempts this year, using methods such as fake job interviews, booby-trapped developer tools and fake video-call apps. Some reports link the group behind the theft to North Korea.

The case matters because many companies are giving internal AI assistants broad access to code, tickets and machines. Security commentators note that this may be the first billion-dollar theft in which such a tool served as a stepping stone between computers, though that is analysis rather than something Binance has confirmed.

Several questions are still open. Binance has not explained how an outsider was able to use its own AI tool to move from one engineer's computer to another. It has not named the AI coding product that was impersonated in June. And outside observers have asked why a deployment token was sitting on an engineer's laptop at all. Until those details are public, the main lesson is that the weakest link was human trust, not the blockchain itself.

items.title: Ted Schlein’s Ballistic Ventures seeks $490M for new funds amid AI-driven cybersecurity boom
items.summary: Ballistic Ventures, the cybersecurity-focused venture firm co-founded by ex-Kleiner Perkins partner Ted Schlein, has filed with the SEC to raise a combined $490 million: $360 million for its third flagship fund and $130 million for a separate vehicle called Fund B. The filings were made as AI reshapes both cyberattacks and security startups.
items.articleBody:
Ballistic Ventures, the San Francisco cybersecurity investor co-founded by former Kleiner Perkins partner Ted Schlein, is seeking to raise $490 million across two new funds, according to filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission that TechCrunch reviewed in the first week of November.

The larger piece is $360 million for the firm's third flagship fund, the same size as the fund it raised in 2024. The remaining $130 million is for a separate vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund B. According to PitchBook data, Ballistic also raised about $130 million for an earlier independent vehicle, Fund A, and Fund B is targeting a similar amount. Neither new fund had recorded any sales when the paperwork was filed, so the figures are targets, not money already committed. The firm declined to comment on its plans.

Ballistic was founded in late 2021 by Schlein, Barmak Meftah, the former president of AT&T Cybersecurity, and Roger Thornton, who co-founded Fortify Software and AlienVault. It announced a $300 million debut fund in 2022 and raised $360 million for its second flagship fund two years later. The firm invests only in cybersecurity startups. Its portfolio has included Talon Cyber Security, later acquired by Palo Alto Networks, and Pangea, bought by CrowdStrike, along with companies such as Armadin, GetReal, Nudge Security and Oligo Security. A cybersecurity investor at another firm told TechCrunch that Schlein's more than two decades at Kleiner Perkins helps set Ballistic apart from rivals.

The timing reflects a wider shift in the industry. Microsoft's latest Digital Defense Report warned that attackers are increasingly using AI for phishing, social engineering and malware development, which lets them move faster and at greater scale. At the same time, the spread of AI agents is opening new problems that security startups can try to solve. A JPMorgan Chase report found that AI-enabled companies made up about 72 percent of US cybersecurity venture deals through May of this year, up from 36 percent in 2019.

For founders, the filings signal that dedicated money for security startups is still being raised despite a cautious venture market. For the firm's investors, they show an ambition to keep growing at a steady pace rather than shrink.

Several things are not yet known. The filings do not say what Fund B will focus on or when either fund might close, and Ballistic may not reach its full $490 million. Until the firm makes an announcement, the targets should be read as plans, not completed fundraising.

items.title: The Sideload 050: The phones Samsung and Google won’t make
items.summary: Episode 50 of 9to5Google's The Sideload podcast, with guest Nick Sutrich, looks at why North American and global phone lineups keep diverging, what the market looks like now that OnePlus has left, and how AI, gaming, camera sensors, batteries and modular accessories could shape the next generation of phones.
items.articleBody:
9to5Google has published episode 50 of its podcast The Sideload, titled "The phones Samsung and Google won't make." Hosts Will and Daniel are joined by guest Nick Sutrich. The episode runs about an hour and was released on November 3.

According to 9to5Google's description, the conversation starts from a familiar frustration: the ever-present split between the phones sold in North America and those sold elsewhere. It then looks at what the market is like now that OnePlus is gone, and closes on the idea that a future smartphone could replace a handheld gaming device such as the Steam Deck.

The published timecodes show the topics in order: the state of the market, AI and gaming, camera sensors, batteries, and modular camera accessories, followed by a wrap-up.

The OnePlus discussion has real news behind it. OnePlus confirmed on July 16 that it would stop launching new phones in North America and Europe, with the OnePlus 15 as its last release in both regions and remaining stock selling until it runs out. The brand is expected to continue in China and India, and its phones are set to move from its own OxygenOS to Oppo's ColorOS. Oppo has said it has no plans to sell phones in the US, so the move removes the whole Oppo family from that market. Analysts also note that OnePlus never held more than about 3 percent of the US market, even at its peak in 2021.

The wider market is under strain. Counterpoint Research reported that global smartphone shipments fell 11 percent year over year in the second quarter of 2026, the weakest April to June quarter since 2013, and expects average phone prices to rise about 6.9 percent this year as memory costs climb. Apple and Samsung continue to dominate the US market.

Against that backdrop, the episode's other topics are about where phone makers could still compete: more capable gaming and on-device AI, larger camera sensors, better batteries, and add-on camera hardware.

The episode is available on YouTube and in 9to5Google's podcast feeds. Readers who want the hosts' specific views on which phones brands should build, and why, will need to listen to the full conversation, because the show notes only outline the topics.

items.title: Reddit is testing in-app search ads as traffic from Google declines
items.summary: Reddit has begun a limited test of ads inside its in-app search results, aiming at people who search the platform for buying advice. The test follows a drop in referrals from Google, which Reddit blames on Google's AI-powered search.
items.articleBody:
Reddit has started testing ads in the search results inside its app, the company announced on Tuesday, November 3. The test comes as the platform deals with falling traffic from Google and looks for more ways to earn money from the people who already use it.

The ads will appear in search results based mainly on how relevant they are to the query. Reddit's own examples are a search for "espresso station" showing ads for mugs, beans or espresso machines, and a search for "home office setup" showing ads for monitors, desks and chairs. In screenshots Reddit shared, the ads sit near the top of the results with a small ad marker. Reddit says search results pages already have high purchase and search intent, because many people use them to look for recommendations and buying advice.

This is only an initial test. Reddit says a limited group of eligible advertisers will have access at first, and it plans to study how users respond so it can refine the experience over time. It has not said how often the ads will appear, and it suggests the format may expand later.

The background is a traffic problem. In its third-quarter update, Reddit said search referrals fell by more than one million per week on average in October. CEO Steve Huffman has pointed to Google's AI features, including AI Mode, which answer questions on the results page and send fewer visitors to other sites. Reddit also issued a fourth-quarter revenue forecast that fell short of expectations and warned that daily users in the United States could decline by a low double-digit percentage in the quarter if the trend continues.

Reddit is also planning a gradual move toward a logged-in experience, starting in markets outside the United States. Visitors who used to read discussions through Google without an account may eventually need to sign in to view some of them. Analysts see the search ads and the login push as two responses to the same decline. Separate industry figures from eMarketer show Google referrals to large publishers fell 43 percent year over year between June 2025 and 2026, and 59.8 percent for small publishers, so the pressure is not unique to Reddit.

For advertisers, the new placement offers a way to reach shoppers while they are researching products, especially categories where reviews and recommendations matter. For everyday users, it means more promoted content mixed into results they use to find honest opinions, which could affect how much they trust search on the platform.

Several questions remain. Reddit has not said how many ads users will see, when more advertisers will get access, or what results the test produces. It is also unclear whether search ads and mandatory sign-ins will be enough to make up for the lost Google traffic.

items.title: Here’s what it’s like to use Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch
items.summary: Apple's first watchOS 27.3 developer beta brings two Audio Intelligence features, Live Rewind and Siri Recap, to the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Both are opt-in, both are still in beta, and Apple says no audio is ever recorded or stored.
items.articleBody:
Apple has put its new Audio Intelligence features for the Apple Watch into developer testing. The company released the first developer betas of watchOS 27.3 and iOS 27.3 on Tuesday, November 3. The features were first announced at Apple's September hardware event, where the company said they would arrive in beta later this year.

Audio Intelligence is a group of four features. Sound Recognition and Shazam music recognition are already on the watch, so the new additions in the beta are Live Rewind and Siri Recap.

Live Rewind produces a text transcript of the last 15 seconds of speech picked up by the watch's microphone. Apple says it only activates when the user presses the Digital Crown, and it plays an audible chime from the speaker even when the watch is in silent mode.

Siri Recap works in the background. It uses ambient listening to detect conversations the wearer is part of, and after a conversation ends, Apple Intelligence generates a title and a short list of key points. These appear in the Siri app on the iPhone. They are not full transcripts and do not say who said what. Reports say recaps can be set to delete automatically after up to seven days unless the user saves them, that sensitive details such as financial or authentication data are not logged, and that users can choose times or places where the feature stays off.

Because the features listen for speech, privacy is the central question. Apple says Audio Intelligence does not create or store audio recordings, and that the raw audio used for processing is not accessible to the operating system, apps, the user or Apple. The processing runs inside the Secure Exclave on the S11 chip, a hardware-isolated area that handles audio separately and deletes it immediately. Both new features are opt-in. Early accounts say they are off by default and must be turned on from the Watch app on the iPhone. Apple has published a privacy overview and a support article describing the controls and limits.

Availability is narrow. The features require an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4, which have the S11 chip. They also need a paired iPhone 16 or later that supports Apple Intelligence and Siri AI; the iPhone 16e is excluded. Owners of older Apple Watch models cannot use either feature even after updating to watchOS 27.3. The software is currently available only to developers, and reports expect the public release of watchOS 27.3 in December alongside iOS 27.3.

The launch lands in an ongoing debate about wearables that listen to the world around them. Apple's approach relies on opt-in settings, short audio buffers, no persistent raw recordings and, for Live Rewind, an audible cue. Because this is a first beta, behavior and details could change before release, and how well the summaries work in everyday conversations is still to be proven.

items.title: Google Messages redesigning pinned chats and moving search
items.summary: Google Messages is testing a homepage redesign in its Android beta. Pinned chats become large contact photos above the whole conversation list, search moves to a floating button next to "Start chat" for easier one-handed use, and the Gemini shortcut moves to the top-right corner. There is no release date yet.
items.articleBody:
Google is testing a significant homepage redesign for Google Messages on Android, according to reporting that began on November 3. The changes are in the app's beta channel and are reaching testers in stages, so they are not widely available. They arrive alongside the app's new blue gradient icon, which matches Google's updated G logo.

The most visible change involves pinned chats. Today they sit at the top of the conversation list. In the test, they are lifted above all conversations and shown as large contact photos, using the background layer that currently holds the Messages wordmark, search and account menu. This pushes the rest of the conversation list further down the page. As in iMessage on iOS, the pinned area does not show message history or the last message sent.

The second change moves search. Instead of a search bar at the top of the screen, search becomes a centered floating button beside the "Start chat" button. At the top of the list, the pair appears as a magnifying-glass icon and a "Start chat" pill. When the user scrolls down, search expands into a pill-shaped "Search" button and the other button shrinks, with an animation that reviewers describe as smooth. Placing search near the thumb should help on large phones, where reaching the top of the screen is awkward.

The Gemini shortcut is also affected. Early reports said it was unclear whether the Gemini floating button would remain. A later report says Google has replaced it with a button in the top-right corner next to the profile picture, similar to the design used in Google Workspace apps. Google has not announced where it will ultimately end up.

Early feedback is mixed. Android Central, citing beta testers, argued that heavy texters may dislike the new layout, because large pinned photos push recent conversations lower and require more scrolling. It suggested Google offer a choice between compact and expanded pinned chats. Reports say someone with only two pinned chats may barely notice the difference. The exact number of pinned chats the layout supports has not been confirmed.

Google has not announced a stable release date, and as with any beta test, the design could change or be dropped before it reaches everyone. For now, the redesign shows Google trying to make Messages easier to use with one hand while keeping favorite contacts a tap away. Whether those gains outweigh the loss of conversation previews for pinned chats is still to be settled.

items.title: What type of battery does the Slate Truck use?
items.summary: Slate's budget electric pickup now uses a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery made by Gotion in Illinois, replacing the nickel-based (NMC) pack from SK On in Georgia that the company originally planned. The change helps Slate keep its $24,950 starting price and lifts projected range to 205 miles.
items.articleBody:
Slate's stripped-down electric pickup, the truck backed by Jeff Bezos that is meant to be one of the cheapest EVs in the US, will use a different battery than the one the company first announced. Instead of a nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) pack, it will use a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) pack built by Gotion at its plant in Manteno, Illinois.

When Slate unveiled the truck in April 2025, the base model was to carry a 52.7 kWh NMC battery from South Korea's SK On, made in Georgia, with an estimated range of about 150 miles. Buyers who paid more were to get an 84.3 kWh pack rated at about 240 miles. Slate has since dropped that two-battery plan in favor of a single 65 kWh LFP pack with a projected range of 205 miles. The company says the truck keeps its advertised starting price of $24,950, plus a $1,450 destination fee.

The company announced the change in June 2026. Slate executives said that when the project began around 2022, there were few LFP options. LFP supply is concentrated in China, and early on the company worried about federal EV tax credit rules that limited battery components linked to "foreign entities of concern." Slate CEO Chris Barman has said a supplier it considered earlier lacked the capacity it needed and could not meet those sourcing rules. Since then, more LFP production has become available in the US, and Gotion can now build the pack in Illinois, about 90 miles from Slate's factory in Warsaw, Indiana.

Cost is the main reason. The battery is the most expensive component in any EV, and LFP cells are generally cheaper than NMC cells. One analysis puts the difference at roughly 40 percent. LFP is also less energy dense, but a cell-to-pack design, which removes some of the intermediate packaging, helped Slate raise the projected range instead of lowering it.

Gotion is a Hefei, China-based company, and its involvement has drawn attention because the LFP supply chain is dominated by Chinese firms. Some commentators note the switch came after the federal EV tax credit rules that shaped Slate's original choice were changed, while other coverage claims the truck still qualifies for credits. These accounts conflict, so buyers should check eligibility rather than assume it.

Several things are still unclear. Slate had said it would ship the truck later this year, and reports do not confirm current delivery timing. Analysts also point to supplier concentration as a risk: if Gotion's Illinois plant faces delays or quality problems, Slate's production could be affected. For now, the switch shows how a startup chasing a very low price is willing to rework its supply chain to get there.

items.title: Orbital Matter 3D-printed the first rigid beam in the vacuum of space
items.summary: European startup Orbital Matter says its Replicator 2 satellite has 3D-printed a half-meter rigid beam in the open vacuum of orbit, which it calls a first for a free-flying spacecraft. The company says the technique could eventually be used to build large solar arrays and radiators, such as those proposed for orbital data centers.
items.articleBody:
Orbital Matter, a European startup, says its Replicator 2 satellite has 3D-printed a rigid beam about half a meter long in the vacuum of space. The company calls it a first for a free-flying spacecraft. Earlier 3D printing in microgravity was done inside the pressurized, temperature-controlled cabin of the International Space Station, while Replicator 2's printers operated outside, exposed to vacuum, microgravity and extreme temperature swings.

The satellite carries four printers. Each one makes a rigid cylindrical beam by extruding coils of a custom resin that is hardened with ultraviolet light, a process the company compares to how cement sets after mixing with water. According to reports, one of the four printers suffered an anomaly, but a beam that was printed successfully was used to deploy a solar array. Reports say Replicator 2 launched in July on a SpaceX Transporter mission, and the company announced the result on November 3.

The reason this matters is size. Future spacecraft will need larger solar arrays to generate more electrical power and larger radiators to shed heat into space, especially if they are to serve as orbital data centers. Today, anything that goes to orbit must fit inside a rocket fairing, which means folding structures and adding hinges and deployment mechanisms. Printing structures in orbit could remove that limit. "Replicator 2 is the first proof that we can simply build the array in space, at whatever size the mission demands," said CEO and co-founder Jakub Stojek.

Orbital Matter was co-founded in 2022 by Stojek and Robert Ihnatsin, who previously worked at 3D-printing company Formlabs, and has raised a $3 million seed round. It is working with the European Space Agency and satellite manufacturer Thales Alenia, and says other satellite builders are evaluating its printer-assisted deployment system for panels, antennas and other components. The company plans a larger demonstration in 2028 and hopes to deploy very large solar arrays on satellites by 2030.

Experts and observers urge caution. The beam is short, and its length is currently limited by the resin carried on the satellite. Engineers say beams up to 100 meters long are possible, but that remains a goal, and commentators note that scaling up is unproven. Similar beams were produced in 2023 by NASA-backed Redwire in a vacuum chamber on Earth, but that test never flew in space.

Still to be shown is whether printed booms can be made repeatedly and reliably at much larger sizes, how they hold up over years of thermal cycling, and whether space-based data centers become a real market. For now, the result is a small but concrete step toward building large structures in orbit rather than launching them whole.

items.title: ChatGPT has hit roughly 20% of Google Search volume, OpenAI says
items.summary: OpenAI says ChatGPT now handles roughly one-fifth as many search-like queries as Google, a figure shared by ChatGPT product lead Adam Fry. OpenAI has not published the data or explained how it counts a search, and independent estimates are lower.
items.articleBody:
OpenAI says ChatGPT's search activity has grown to roughly one-fifth of the volume of queries handled by Google. The figure came from Adam Fry, who leads consumer product for ChatGPT, who shared it at an OpenAI-hosted event in New York on Monday, November 2, and in a conversation with Alex Kantrowitz of Big Technology. Fry described ChatGPT's volume of search-like queries as roughly 20 percent of Google's.

The number comes with caveats. It is OpenAI's own claim, and the company has not published the data behind it. It has not said which Google figure it compared against or exactly how it counts a search. According to OpenAI, every question that makes ChatGPT search the web counts as a search, so twenty prompts in one conversation that each trigger a web search would count as twenty searches, while quick answers that do not need the web are not counted. The comparison is about query volume, not about ChatGPT's share of the search market.

Outside estimates are lower. Ahrefs estimated in February that ChatGPT gets about 12 percent of Google's search volume, and SEO software company SEOClarity put it nearer 7.5 percent, or roughly 375 billion queries a year. Applying OpenAI's 20 percent to Google's last disclosed annual volume of more than 5 trillion searches would put ChatGPT above one trillion search-like queries a year, but the two companies have not shown that they count searches in the same way.

The statement came alongside other growth claims. Fry said ChatGPT's weekly active users rose from 1 billion to 1.2 billion in about two months. OpenAI is also working on a more interactive "intelligent UI" and has begun showing images of sponsored products in ChatGPT. Fry said ads have not hurt the product or its usage. Reports note that Bing, by comparison, holds roughly 5 percent of the search market.

Google is not standing still. Google reported its fastest query growth in five years in the same week, and it has acknowledged that its own push into AI-powered search brings "lower monetization." For marketers, conversational queries tend to be longer and reveal more intent, but neither OpenAI nor Google breaks out conversational query volume, ad load or click-through rates in a way advertisers can benchmark.

The main takeaway is that ChatGPT has become a serious place where people look things up, whatever the exact percentage. What is still unknown is how many of those queries truly replace a Google search, how the numbers compare when counted the same way, and whether the growth will continue as ads arrive in ChatGPT.

items.title: Sonos' new voice assistant is launching in early access on November 6
items.summary: Sonos will open early access to its new AI voice assistant, Sonos 27voice, on November 6. The test is limited to approved US users in English, and the company says a smaller group will help it gather feedback before a wider 2027 release.
items.articleBody:
Sonos says its new voice assistant, Sonos 27voice, will open for early-access testing on November 6. Access comes through an app update that began rolling out the week of November 3, and the company plans a full release in 2027.

The early-access program is deliberately narrow. Sonos 27voice is available only in the United States and only in English at first. Users cannot simply switch it on: they must request access in the Sonos app, under Settings, General Settings and Voice Assistants, and be approved. Reports say approved testers begin getting access from November 12. It also requires S2 speakers running the Sonos 27 software.

Sonos introduced Sonos 27 in September and said the assistant could help with "music and mood curation." Like the older Voice Control, 27voice can control playback across the speakers in a user's system. It also handles timers, weather and supported smart home accessories, and Sonos has described it as able to understand more natural, conversational requests, such as moving music between rooms or playing an artist's newest album. The company has also highlighted support for third-party AI assistants such as ChatGPT and custom agents.

The slow rollout appears to be a lesson from the past. Industry coverage notes that Sonos is testing with a smaller group before a full release in order to collect feedback, and that this is likely meant to avoid the backlash that followed its 2024 app redesign. Giving a limited group early access lets the company find problems before millions of owners see them.

Privacy is a key consideration. Unlike Sonos's earlier Voice Control, 27voice processes requests through cloud servers, and reports say some open-ended questions may use outside AI models. Sonos says the assistant is optional: owners can stay on Classic Voice Control or leave 27voice at any time, and Sonos says 27voice and Amazon Alexa can be active on the same compatible speaker.

The same update added Presets, a long-requested feature that saves a room, music and volume for one-tap playback, along with small interface changes. Presets do not depend on 27voice.

What remains unknown is how many people will be admitted to the early-access group, how well the assistant handles real household use, how Sonos will handle voice data over time, and when the assistant will reach other countries and languages.

items.title: Google will disable Search for students unless schools accept AI features in ‘Guided Learning’ push
items.summary: Google will turn off Gemini and Search by default for K-12 student accounts unless school administrators switch them on, and schools that want Search will have to accept its built-in AI features. Google says Search and AI are too closely tied to separate. It is also rolling out its Guided Learning tool, which is designed to walk students through problems instead of handing over answers.
items.articleBody:
Google has announced a change to how schools manage its AI products, and it comes with a significant catch: schools that want to block Google's AI features entirely will also lose access to Google Search for their students. The announcement was made on Tuesday, November 3, in a blog post by Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education.

Under the new policy, Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search will be turned off by default for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on. Google describes the aim as giving school leaders control and confidence to use AI in classrooms as they see fit. Reports say the change takes effect next year, with two options expected in early 2027: a Search experience that includes AI Overviews and other AI features, and one where Guided Learning replaces them.

What administrators cannot do is keep traditional Search while switching off the AI. Phillips told The New York Times that Search and AI are deeply integrated. Students at schools that disable AI will not be able to search and will see a message from their school saying it is unavailable.

The change was announced alongside Guided Learning, a feature designed to help students work through problems step by step instead of skipping straight to answers. It became available worldwide in Google Classroom on Tuesday, and Google plans to test it in Search at select US schools, with broader availability in the coming months. Google also pointed to research in which students who used Guided Learning improved their test scores by 8.1 percentage points, compared with 5.3 points for students using regular web tools. The detail of that study was not described in the coverage reviewed.

The announcement drew quick criticism from educators and policymakers. Critics argue that Google is using its dominance in search to push schools toward AI and leaving them no real way to opt out. The central concern is that teachers may not want students relying on AI Overviews to research or complete assignments but still want them to be able to find sources and learning materials through a search engine. The announcement also comes amid wider worry that AI chatbots undermine learning by giving direct answers.

Several questions remain. It is not yet clear how many schools will accept AI features to keep Search, whether the Guided Learning version of Search will satisfy those wanting a more restricted experience, and whether regulators or school districts will push back. Google has also not said whether it will ever offer a version of Search for students with the AI features removed.

items.title: iPhone 18 rumors suggest a bigger battery, higher price next year
items.summary: A Weibo post from leaker Digital Chat Station claims Apple's standard iPhone 18 will have a larger battery than the iPhone 17 and could cost more. The post gives no battery size or price, Apple has confirmed nothing, and the phone is expected in the first half of 2027.
items.articleBody:
A new rumor says Apple's standard iPhone 18 will have a bigger battery than the current iPhone 17 and may also be more expensive. It comes from the Chinese leaker known as Digital Chat Station, who posted on Weibo in early November. Apple has not confirmed any of it.

The leaker did not give a battery capacity or a price. For comparison, the iPhone 17 has a 3,692 mAh battery. Apple already raised capacities in this year's iPhone 18 Pro models, which reportedly carry cells of about 4,056 mAh in the Pro and 5,391 mAh in the Pro Max for versions with a physical SIM tray, up roughly 1.7 percent and 11.8 percent from their iPhone 17 Pro counterparts. Apple has generally increased battery size from one generation to the next, so a larger cell in the base model is plausible.

The price claim is vaguer still. Digital Chat Station suggested the iPhone 18 could cost more, but did not say by how much, in which markets, or compared with what. Earlier this year Apple raised the US starting price of the iPhone 17 by $100 to $899, and some competitors made similar increases, which is why another rise would not surprise many buyers. Some outlets point out that the leaker framed the price increase as a possibility, not as a fact.

The same post lists other specifications that have been reported before. The standard iPhone 18 is said to have a 6.3-inch OLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate, the regular Dynamic Island rather than the smaller version on the Pro models, a 2nm A20 chip, Face ID and a 48-megapixel dual-camera system. A newer, more efficient chip together with a larger battery could noticeably improve battery life.

Timing also matters. Apple released only its Pro models this fall, and the standard iPhone 18 is expected in the first half of 2027, reportedly alongside the iPhone 18e and a second-generation iPhone Air. Digital Chat Station predicts the standard iPhone 18 will be the best seller of the three.

The leaker has a solid record on displays and chips, but observers note that battery sizes and especially prices are often not final this far ahead of launch, and that Digital Chat Station has recently reposted older rumors as new. For buyers, the practical question is whether to buy an iPhone 17 now or wait for what may be a longer-lasting but more expensive phone. Until Apple announces the device, the battery size, price and launch date should be treated as unconfirmed.

items.title: Apple starts giving Siri AI access to third-party apps
items.summary: Apple has opened its new Siri AI to every third-party developer through the iOS 27.3 developer betas, letting apps expose content and actions to the assistant via App Intents. It is a developer preview only: apps using the feature are expected to reach customers in 2027, after an App Store submission window opens in spring.
items.articleBody:
Apple has opened its upgraded Siri AI assistant to every third-party developer. The change arrived on Tuesday, November 3, as part of the first iOS 27.3 developer beta, along with matching betas for iPadOS, macOS and visionOS 27.3. It is a developer preview. Regular iPhone users will not see third-party Siri AI features yet.

Until now, only a smaller set of apps had deep connections to the assistant, and Siri could reach third-party apps mainly through predefined app schemas. Under the new preview, any app can bring its own content and custom actions into Siri AI using App Intents, the framework apps already use to expose features to the system. Apple said the preview lets apps tap into Siri AI's newest abilities, including understanding personal context, awareness of what is on the screen, and natural language.

Developers can also build what Apple calls "skills." These are Markdown files that teach Siri AI multi-step workflows, so that one request can chain several actions without the user switching between apps. Developer-focused coverage says a single code annotation can turn an existing app action into a tool that Siri can call. Apple notes that the App Intents API and Siri's behavior may change during the preview.

For users, the idea is to ask Siri to do things inside the apps they already use, not only Apple's. Examples Apple lists include checking on a delivery, booking a reservation or placing an order once those apps adopt the new tools. Apple's own examples of what Siri AI can do with personal context include finding a coffee shop you visited last week or archiving files you have not opened in more than a year.

Timing matters. Apple says apps using the new capabilities are expected to reach customers in 2027, and developers can submit them to the App Store beginning in spring. iOS 27.3 itself is expected to reach the public in December. One report stresses that no third-party app ships the new skills feature to customers today, and that the public release will not include a switch for it.

Some coverage also points to a transition for older code. One developer guide says the older SiriKit framework still compiles but no longer does anything on iOS 27 devices, so developers supporting both iOS 26 and iOS 27 may need both approaches. That claim comes from a single developer-focused source, so developers should check Apple's documentation.

What is not yet known is how well Siri AI will handle real third-party actions, how many developers will adopt it quickly, and what privacy and permission controls users will see when an assistant can act inside many apps. Those answers should emerge as the beta progresses and apps begin shipping next year.

items.title: Netflix thinks AI might save you from scrolling aimlessly for something to watch
items.summary: Netflix has begun testing "AI Discover," a new tab in its TV app that suggests titles through AI-generated themes such as "Something Light" or "Scare Me." It is initially limited to a small group of US members and is described as a testing ground for features that could reach the main app.
items.articleBody:
Netflix has started testing a new way to choose what to watch. On Tuesday, November 3, the company announced "AI Discover," a new tab in its TV app that uses AI-generated themes to help viewers decide, instead of making them scroll through rows of titles.

Opening the tab shows a handful of themes, each paired with a clip from a show or movie. Examples include "Something Light," "Scare Me," "Family Movie Night" and "Quick Watches." After you pick one, Netflix offers more specific themes so you can narrow the choice, and a "Something Different" option brings up a fresh set of picks. Viewers can also refresh the themes or block titles they do not want. In this first version there is no box for typing a request. You click through the suggestions. Netflix says AI helps create the themes and that it will explain results along the way. It describes the feature as powered by a new intelligence layer that responds to what members say in real time and keeps learning.

AI Discover is deliberately limited at first. It is rolling out to a small group of US members who use English-language profiles on supported TVs, and Netflix says more users will get it in the coming weeks. Not everyone who sees the tab will necessarily see the same thing, because the company plans to try different ideas over time.

Netflix calls AI Discover its "test kitchen," a place to try new recipes for discovery. Feedback will help decide which features are kept, improved, or moved into the main Netflix experience. That gives the company a way to experiment without changing the main homepage for all subscribers overnight.

The feature is the latest in a long run of attempts to shorten the time viewers spend choosing. Netflix has tried a shuffle play option and tested an OpenAI-powered chatbot alongside a redesign last year, and the new tab builds on its AI-powered search on mobile.

Early reaction has been mixed. Some viewers on social media have been skeptical and say they would rather Netflix focus on better titles than on better ways to find them. Supporters say that a tool that lets people guide the process by mood, time or situation could help those who know the kind of thing they want but cannot settle on a title.

For Netflix, the stakes are straightforward. If viewers find something quickly, they are more likely to keep watching, and AI-driven themes could eventually become a bigger part of how everyone browses. What is still unknown is how well the suggestions work in practice, how personalized they are compared with the existing recommendations, and whether the test will expand beyond the US and English.

items.title: Researchers warned of North Korean hacking tactics years before record $6.3B Binance heist
items.summary: Security researchers and government agencies have warned for years that North Korean hackers pose as recruiters and investors to trick employees into running malicious software. Binance, which says it faced at least 57 suspected attacks from North Korea, still lost a record $6.3 billion through that kind of scheme, according to its own account of the breach.
items.articleBody:
The record $6.3 billion theft from Binance used methods that researchers had been warning about for years. According to Binance, North Korean hackers posed as recruiters and approached a software engineer who works on the company's wallets. The FBI and blockchain investigators have blamed North Korea for the heist, although the investigation is still ongoing.

Binance's account describes a months-long social engineering scheme. The attackers used fake social media profiles and the lure of a job to get an employee to download malicious software. During the interview process, the engineer was reportedly given a fake coding assignment, and opening it installed malware that Binance's security tools did not detect. That gave the attackers a foothold they used to reach two more engineers and, eventually, systems that controlled billions of dollars of crypto. The company has said an internal AI tool also played a part in the later stages.

The tactics were well known. Researchers have warned for years that North Korean hackers pose as venture capitalists, investors and recruiters, often using dossiers of stolen American identities to appear convincing and to persuade employees to give them access. These campaigns can run for months, and they have prompted repeated warnings from US authorities and cybersecurity firms. CrowdStrike data referenced alongside the Binance story indicates that about half of intrusions at US tech companies in the prior year were attributed to North Koreans posing as remote IT workers and fake recruiters.

Binance says it had faced at least 57 suspected attacks from North Korea, which it described as a sign of the persistent threat that state-sponsored actors pose to the crypto industry. This one succeeded. North Korea began focusing its hacking operations on cryptocurrency theft around 2017, according to the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, a group of 11 countries that includes the US, South Korea and Japan. The FBI has used the name TraderTraitor for the type of operation behind such attacks. Analysts describe the activity as a revenue stream for the Kim regime, and reports say stolen coins are often turned into cash through over-the-counter traders in China.

Binance has said it will bring in outside cybersecurity experts to review the incident and has added new security measures. A company spokesperson declined to answer questions on the record about how Binance prevents unauthorized or malicious code from running on employee laptops and whether outside parties had audited its network before the hack.

Those unanswered questions are central. If the methods were widely documented, observers will want to know which defenses were in place and why they failed. The answers could shape how other exchanges train staff, restrict code on work devices and handle job-related contacts.

items.title: AI inference startup Fal doubles its valuation to $16B as demand surges
items.summary: San Francisco AI inference startup Fal has raised $1.3 billion in a Series F round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, doubling its valuation to $16 billion in seven months. The company runs image, video and audio AI models for developers, and says demand has outrun its computing capacity.
items.articleBody:
Fal, a San Francisco startup that runs AI image, video and audio models for developers, has raised $1.3 billion in a Series F funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners. The round, announced on November 3, values the five-year-old company at $16 billion, according to Bloomberg and TechCrunch. That is double the $8 billion valuation it had in April.

Nvidia, Sound Ventures, HOF Capital and T. Rowe Price also took part. Fal announced the Series F together with its earlier Series E, which Sequoia led in April with $350 million, and said the two rounds total $1.65 billion. Reports say Fal has raised more than $1.9 billion since its founding in 2021. Bessemer partner Talia Goldberg is joining the board of the company, whose formal name is Features & Labels Inc.

Fal sells what the industry calls inference, the computing work of running a trained model each time someone asks for an image or a video clip. Developers reach thousands of models through a single API, and model makers use the platform to distribute and serve their work. Bessemer lists Adobe, Canva, Shopify, World Labs and Amazon among large companies running production workloads on it. The company says it passed $800 million in annualized revenue earlier this year.

The valuation has climbed quickly. Fal was valued at $1.5 billion after a $125 million Series C led by Meritech in July 2025, at $4.5 billion after a Sequoia-led Series D in December 2025, and at $8 billion in April before this round. The new valuation is roughly 20 times the annualized revenue figure that has been reported.

Demand has been strong enough to cause problems. Fal's CEO has said that in summer 2026 usage grew so fast that the company had to cap what customers could use. The new money is meant to expand computing capacity, and the company plans to grow beyond its current staff of about 185. Bessemer argues that systems built to serve chatbots do not carry over well to video and image models, which have different computing demands.

Fal faces well-funded rivals. Its valuation sits just behind Fireworks AI, which reportedly raised $1.5 billion at a $17.5 billion valuation in July, and it competes with providers such as Baseten and Modal.

Questions remain. Analysts point to margins, customer concentration and reliance on Nvidia hardware as open issues, and note that a roughly 20-times revenue multiple leaves little room for a slowdown in growth. For now, the round shows how aggressively investors are pricing companies that supply the computing behind generative media.
