items.title: Don't throw away your laptop's old SSDs — do this instead
items.summary: A spare SSD from an old laptop can become a portable drive for the price of a cheap USB enclosure. The key is to match the enclosure to the drive's type and size, copy off or wipe any old data, format the drive, and test it before trusting it with anything important.
items.articleBody:
When you upgrade or retire a laptop, the old solid-state drive does not have to go in the bin. In most cases it can be turned into a fast external drive by putting it in a small USB enclosure, usually for much less than the price of a new portable drive. Here is how to do it and what to watch for.

Start by identifying the drive. SSDs in laptops are usually 2.5-inch SATA drives, M.2 SATA drives, or M.2 NVMe drives. The enclosure must match both the form factor and the interface, and an enclosure for M.2 SATA will not necessarily work with an M.2 NVMe drive. Check the label on the drive or look up its model number before buying anything.

Before you touch the drive's contents, think about the data. A drive taken from an old computer may still hold documents, photos, saved games, browser data or an operating system. If you have not already backed it up, connect it through the enclosure first and copy what you need. Once the files are safe, wipe the drive, because formatting erases everything on it, and this matters even more if you ever plan to give the drive away.

Next, choose the enclosure. A basic 2.5-inch SATA enclosure is cheap, and reviewers report paying around ten to twelve dollars for one. NVMe enclosures cost more, with one writer paying about $30 for a 10Gbps aluminum model. Look for USB-C and a rating of at least USB 3.2 Gen 2 if you want speed. Aluminum cases with thermal pads or a heatsink handle heat better than plastic, which can trap it and slow the drive during long transfers. Thunderbolt enclosures are faster but cost more and need a compatible port.

Installation is simple. Open the enclosure, seat the drive, close it, and plug it into your computer with the supplied cable. Then format it in Windows or macOS so the drive is empty and in a format that suits you. Pick a file system based on where you will use it: exFAT works across Windows and Mac, while NTFS or APFS suit a single platform.

Speed depends on the drive, the enclosure's controller, the cable and the port. One guide says SATA SSDs typically reach about 400 to 550MB/s in USB 3.2 enclosures, and NVMe drives can reach around 1,000MB/s in a good USB 3.2 Gen 2 enclosure. Both are well above a typical flash drive.

There are limits. An enclosure cannot repair worn-out flash memory, and a drive that was failing when you removed it should not be used for anything you cannot afford to lose. Test the finished drive before trusting it with a full archive, and keep a second copy of anything irreplaceable.

Used this way, an old SSD makes a useful portable drive for moving files, a backup target for non-critical data, or extra storage for a laptop with a single internal drive. Some people also use one as storage for a game console. It also keeps working hardware out of the waste stream, which is a small but real benefit.

items.title: Want an iPhone Duo for the holidays? Apple’s latest stock update isn’t reassuring
items.summary: Apple says its $1,999 foldable iPhone Duo is supply-constrained and it cannot predict when supply will catch up with demand. New orders already show delivery in late January 2027, so buyers hoping to get one for the holidays may be out of luck.
items.articleBody:
If you were hoping to find Apple's first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo, under the tree this holiday season, Apple's latest update is not encouraging. After the company reported its September-quarter results on November 2, CEO John Ternus told Reuters that the Duo is "constrained as of today" and that Apple is not able to predict when supply and demand will be in balance.

The phone, priced at $1,999, opened for preorders on October 16 and reached stores in late October. Reports say it sold out quickly, with one account saying preorder stock was gone within half an hour and others saying it sold out within a week of launch. Stores have had little stock for walk-in buyers, and some units have been available through online reservations. Orders placed now show delivery estimates in late January 2027, and UBS has said availability will remain limited going into December even though demand looks strong.

Apple's results did not include any Duo sales because the quarter ended before the phone went on sale. The company reported record quarterly revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent, with iPhone revenue up 17 percent to about $57 billion. Ternus said Apple has been "thrilled" with the early response from reviewers and customers and is working hard to get the Duo into customers' hands as quickly as it can.

There is also a quality issue. Apple said it is aware of a problem affecting the inner display on a small number of Duo units and told affected users to contact AppleCare for a replacement. Ternus said a very small percentage of units have been returned and that Apple is replacing them. Some analysts suggest that replacement stock may further strain supply, though that is inference and not an Apple statement.

The supply problem goes beyond the foldable. Apple has pointed to rising memory and chip costs, driven by demand from the AI industry, and said that memory limits will also affect Mac and iPad supply this holiday. Earlier this year Apple raised prices on some MacBooks and iPads by up to 25 percent because of higher hardware and chip costs.

Competitors may benefit. Reports from Korea claim that sales of Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 rose about 20 percent in the week after the Duo became available, though those figures are not confirmed.

For shoppers, the practical advice is to order early if you want a Duo, a Mac or an iPad by the holidays, and to expect delays. Apple has not said when the shortage will end, so late-January delivery dates could slip.

items.title: Itch.io adds a filter for games with gen AI disclosures
items.summary: Itch.io has added a "No AI" search filter that hides games carrying a generative AI disclosure, and says it deleted a couple of terabytes of AI-generated spam. Steam also requires AI disclosures but does not let shoppers filter them out.
items.articleBody:
Indie game marketplace Itch.io has added a "No AI" filter that lets players hide games that carry a generative AI disclosure. The platform announced the change in early November alongside a clean-up, saying on Bluesky that it had deleted a couple of terabytes of AI-generated spam.

Itch.io requires creators to disclose when a game uses generative AI. Selecting "No AI" in search removes any game with such a disclosure from the results, and players can also browse a "No AI" tag page. The filter works from the disclosures, so it is only as reliable as the information developers provide. It does not let developers specify how extensively they used AI, and one user forum notes that the disclosure covers several categories while the filter lumps them together. Itch.io has also extended the disclosure requirement to tabletop games, books, comics and soundtracks.

The platform says the problem is volume. It posted a chart of new game pages created each day, and reports say the number of uploads has as much as doubled in recent months as AI tools have spread. The deleted material included both games and developer assets such as asset packs, although Itch.io did not say how many items were removed. The removal targets spam and bulk uploads of AI creations, such as very large amounts of poorly optimized generated models, and not all games that use generative AI.

Itch.io's move stands out because Steam also requires disclosure on store pages but does not allow players to filter those games out of search. Valve recently admitted that Steam has a problem with AI-generated games and cloning, and some commentators suggested developers may be partly responsible by making games easy to copy.

Reaction has been mostly positive, though some players want Itch.io to go further and ban generative AI assets outright. Others point out how hard it is to draw a line, because an "AI game" could be anything from a low-quality title coded entirely by AI to a project that used AI tools in a small part of development. Some developers argue that marking code partly written with AI as AI content does not help players.

For players, the filter is a simple way to avoid AI-generated content on a platform known for small, personal projects. For developers, it means that disclosing AI use will make a game invisible to a growing group of shoppers. What remains to be seen is whether Itch.io will refine the disclosure categories, whether more sellers will use accurate labels, and whether Steam will respond with a similar filter.

items.title: Reddit tests ads in search results as traffic declines and growth concerns mount
items.summary: Reddit has begun testing ads inside its own search results, a move aimed at earning more from people already on the platform while Google's AI-driven search changes cut the traffic it receives from outside.
items.articleBody:
Reddit has started testing advertisements inside its own search results, announcing the experiment on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. The test comes at a delicate moment for the company. Traffic arriving from outside search engines has weakened, and investors are asking how Reddit will keep growing if that trend continues.

According to screenshots the company shared, the sponsored results appear near the top of the results page when someone searches within Reddit. Reddit did not say how often these ads will show up, which advertisers are taking part, or what they will pay. The company has described the rollout as an early test meant to measure how users and advertisers respond before any wider launch.

The timing is closely tied to Reddit's latest earnings. In its Q3 shareholder letter, published on October 29, the company said search referral traffic was down meaningfully during the quarter. It also warned that daily users could fall by a low-double-digit percentage in Q4 if current search trends continue. Reddit beat Wall Street expectations on revenue and earnings, but it fell short on U.S. user growth, which is why the stock and the wider growth story are under scrutiny.

Reddit's leadership has pointed to Google's AI-powered search features as the most likely cause. When AI summaries answer a question directly on the results page, fewer people click through to the forums and discussion threads that feed those answers. Reddit's conversations have long ranked prominently in Google results, so any drop in outside clicks hits it directly.

Search ads give Reddit another way to earn money from users who are already inside the platform. People who search on Reddit often have clear intent, such as comparing products, looking for recommendations, or researching a purchase. That makes those moments attractive to advertisers. Reddit has also said that on-site search has been growing, so the company is betting that engaged, logged-in users can make up for some of the visitors it loses from Google.

Some caveats apply. Logged-out web visitors, the group most affected by falling search traffic, account for a relatively small share of Reddit's ad revenue. That suggests its income depends more on logged-in and app users than the traffic headlines imply. Reddit has also not said the ads are a direct response to the traffic decline, so that link is analysts' interpretation rather than a stated company strategy.

Still unknown are how widely the ads will roll out, how users will react to sponsored results in a space known for authentic discussion, and whether the added revenue will be enough to offset slower audience growth. Advertisers and marketers will be watching the test closely, since the results could show whether in-platform search can become a major ad channel as AI changes how people find information online.

items.title: Ten years later, ‘Pokémon Go to the polls’ still haunts the internet
items.summary: A joke from Hillary Clinton's 2016 campaign trail has outlasted the election it was meant for. It resurfaced again on U.S. Election Day 2026, ten years on, as a meme that people use both to tease and to encourage voting.
items.articleBody:
Ten years after it was first said, the phrase "Pokémon Go to the polls" is still one of the internet's most durable political jokes. It resurfaced across social media on U.S. Election Day, November 3, 2026, as it has on many Election Days since 2016.

The line comes from Hillary Clinton, then the Democratic presidential nominee, at a campaign rally in Annandale, Virginia, on July 14, 2016. Speaking about jobs in technology and app development, she said she did not know who had created Pokémon Go but wanted to find out how to get them to have "Pokémon Go to the polls." The remark was meant as a pitch to young voters. It quickly became a meme, and one that many people read as a clumsy attempt to connect with a younger audience.

A decade later, the meme has taken on a different tone. Much of the original mockery has faded, and the phrase now works as a kind of shorthand for the 2016 moment itself. People use it to joke about the optimism of that summer, to nudge friends and followers to vote, and to express a more weary determination to keep showing up despite political fatigue. Because the joke is no longer tied to one side, people across the political spectrum share it.

The technology world it referred to has also changed. Pokémon Go launched in the summer of 2016 and became a global phenomenon, and it still has a dedicated player base and regular in-person events. The game has since changed hands. According to TechCrunch's reporting, it is now owned by a company wholly owned by Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund. Apps are also increasingly written with help from AI tools, a shift that was barely imaginable when Clinton spoke.

Part of the meme's staying power is the way the internet has changed. In 2016, a joke could move between Facebook, Twitter and Tumblr and reach nearly everyone at once. Today attention is split across many platforms, so shared reference points like this one are rarer, which may be why people hold on to it.

It is hard to say exactly why the joke still lands. Some people use it to poke fun at an out-of-touch politician, others as a sign of solidarity among voters who keep turning out even as they grow more cynical. Either way, the phrase has outlived the campaign that produced it and the election it was meant to influence. It is now a small piece of internet history that returns every time Election Day comes around.

items.title: Your Apple Watch has 2 new controversial listening features – but you have to opt in
items.summary: Apple has started rolling out Siri Recap and Live Rewind, two Apple Watch features that use the microphone to help you recall conversations. Both are opt-in, but because they depend on the watch listening for sound, they have raised privacy questions.
items.articleBody:
Apple has begun making two of its most debated Apple Watch features available: Siri Recap and Live Rewind. Both were announced in September as part of the company's Audio Intelligence tools for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. They are now appearing for testers through the watchOS 27.3 developer beta. Because they work by using the watch's microphones, they have been described as "always-listening" features, and that label has made them controversial.

Live Rewind is designed to help when you miss something someone has just said. The watch keeps a rolling buffer of about 15 seconds of ambient audio that is constantly overwritten. When you double-press the Digital Crown, the watch shows a text transcript of those last 15 seconds. Apple suggests uses such as catching a recipe step or a book recommendation mentioned in passing. The transcription is handled with the help of the paired iPhone, so the feature does not work if the phone is out of wireless range.

Siri Recap works differently. Instead of transcribing speech on demand, it is meant to summarize conversations to help you remember them later. It can be turned on or off, and it can be limited by time or location, for example so that it runs only at work. It can also be toggled from Control Center once enabled.

Apple stresses that both features are opt-in and can be switched off again. The company says raw audio is not recorded, is not accessible to apps or to Apple, and is deleted after processing. Live Rewind also plays a chime and shows a full-screen visual when it is used, so nearby people have some warning. Reviewers have noted a limit to that, since the transcript can include words spoken before the alert, so someone close by could still be caught off guard.

The controversy centers on bystanders more than on the wearer. A person who chooses to enable these features agrees to the listening, but the people around them have not. Privacy commentators have also raised legal questions in places where all parties must consent to the recording of a conversation. Some observers have pointed out that, once enabled, Live Rewind has no separate on/off switch for everyday use and is always ready to respond, even though it stores only a few seconds of audio.

Supporters of Apple's approach say the safeguards are stronger than those of a typical voice recorder or cloud transcription app, with on-device processing, short retention and visible alerts. Critics say normalizing microphones that are always ready may be a concern in itself, especially as other companies, including Meta, explore similar wearable AI products.

For now, anyone who does not want the feature can leave it disabled, since nothing is switched on by default. What remains unclear is how widely people will adopt these tools, how courts and regulators will treat them, and whether the privacy protections hold up as the features reach more users.

items.title: How to use your phone to find hidden cameras
items.summary: Staying in a rental or hotel can leave you wondering whether someone is watching. A few simple checks using only your smartphone can help you spot hidden cameras, although none of them is a guarantee.
items.articleBody:
Hidden cameras in short-term rentals, hotel rooms and changing areas are a real privacy concern, and many travelers want a way to check without buying special equipment. Your smartphone can help with several quick checks. None of them is foolproof, but together they can give you a reasonable degree of reassurance.

Start with a visual sweep. Hidden cameras are often placed in objects that face the bed, bathroom or seating areas, such as smoke detectors, clocks, USB chargers, air purifiers, picture frames, plants and TV set-top boxes. Look for tiny holes, odd lens-like dots, or devices that seem out of place or pointed at you. Turning off the lights and using your phone's flashlight can help. A camera lens often reflects light with a small bright glint when you scan the room slowly.

Next, use your phone's camera to check for infrared light. Many cameras that work in the dark use infrared LEDs, which the human eye cannot see. In a dark room, open your camera app and slowly pan across the room. Look for small purple or white glowing dots. Results vary by phone, because some rear cameras filter out infrared. Pointing a TV remote at your camera and pressing a button is an easy test. If you see the remote's light on screen, your camera can pick up infrared. The front camera often works better for this.

Check the Wi-Fi network as well. Many hidden cameras connect to the local network to stream or store video. Network scanner apps can list devices that are connected to the Wi-Fi network, and you can look for unfamiliar names or device types such as cameras. This is only useful if you are allowed to join the network, and it will not catch cameras that record to a memory card or use their own connection.

Mirrors deserve a quick look too. To test a mirror, touch the surface with a fingernail. On a normal mirror, there is a gap between your nail and its reflection. On a two-way mirror, the reflection seems to touch your nail directly. This is a common check, but it is not conclusive on its own.

You can also try dedicated tools. Small radio-frequency detectors and lens finders are sold online, and some people find them useful as a second check. Their quality varies widely, so treat them as a supplement and not as proof.

If you find something suspicious, avoid tampering with it. Take photos or video of the device and where it was found, leave it in place if possible, and contact the property host, the platform you booked with, or local police. If you feel unsafe, leave the room or property first. Recording people in private spaces without their knowledge is illegal in many places, and rental platforms generally prohibit cameras inside bedrooms and bathrooms.

It is worth keeping the risk in perspective. Most rentals and hotels do not have hidden cameras, and a failed check does not prove a room is clear. Still, a few minutes of checking when you arrive is a cheap way to feel more confident about your privacy.

items.title: Ferrari’s controversial Luce EV is sold out for 2027
items.summary: Ferrari says every Luce it plans to build next year already has a buyer, even though the brand's first all-electric car drew heavy criticism over its design when it was unveiled.
items.articleBody:
Ferrari's first all-electric car, the Luce, is already sold out for 2027, according to CEO Benedetto Vigna. He shared the news on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, during the company's third-quarter earnings call. In practical terms, "fully allocated" means that every Luce the carmaker plans to build next year already has a buyer.

The announcement stands out because the Luce has been one of the most polarizing cars in Ferrari's history. When it was revealed in May, its unconventional design drew strong criticism online, and some commentators likened it to a "Magic Mouse on wheels." Fortune reported that even Ferrari's former chairman had warned that the electric model could damage the brand's reputation. The sold-out allocation suggests that these objections have not put off Ferrari's customers.

The car is far from an entry-level product. The Luce starts at around $615,000 and is reported to produce about 1,035 horsepower. Ferrari's customers are typically long-standing clients who are invited to order limited-production models, which helps explain why demand can be secured well before most people have seen the car in person. Reports say buyers have not yet driven the Luce, and Vigna said client test drives planned for next year could further boost demand.

For anyone who has not already ordered one, the wait is long. Reports indicate that new customers now face delivery in 2028. Vigna told journalists that the company has no critical issues on either the manufacturing or the demand side.

There are limits to what the announcement tells us. Ferrari did not say how many Lucs it plans to build in 2027, and it did not provide a regional breakdown of orders. Without those numbers, it is hard to judge how large the sold-out run really is. Ferrari has also traditionally kept production deliberately limited, so a sold-out allocation does not necessarily mean the model will be a high-volume success.

The news matters because Ferrari's move into electric cars has been watched closely by the wider luxury and auto industries. Many traditional performance brands have worried that an EV would dilute what their cars stand for. The early order book suggests that, at least among Ferrari's wealthy clientele, the electric badge has not been a barrier. Whether that holds once the first customers take delivery and the car is judged on the road remains to be seen.

items.title: mSecure Warns Users to Change Passwords, Reset 2FA and Passkeys After Suspicious Activity
items.summary: The company behind the mSecure password manager has told current and former customers to change their master password and stored logins, reset two-factor authentication and replace passkeys after it detected suspicious activity, but it has not said exactly what happened.
items.articleBody:
mSeven Software, the developer of the mSecure password manager, has warned current and former customers to take steps to protect the sensitive information stored in the app. In an email sent on November 3, 2026, the company said it had recently learned of "suspicious activity" connected to mSecure and recommended that users change their passwords, reset their two-factor authentication and replace or remove their passkeys.

The company framed its advice as standard best practice. It recommended that customers change their master password, change the important passwords stored in the vault, reset their two-factor authentication methods and replace passkeys along with any other sensitive information. The warning went to both current and former customers, which suggests that people who no longer use the app may also be affected.

What the email did not do is explain the incident. Security outlets including The Register pointed out that the company did not say what had been compromised, how the activity was detected, or whether any customer data was actually accessed. Some reporting, including coverage by BleepingComputer and TechRadar, says an encrypted customer database stored in the cloud may have been exposed. That detail comes from secondary reporting and has not been confirmed in the company's own message as far as the public record shows, so it should be treated with caution.

The advice matters because a password manager sits at the center of a person's online security. It typically holds logins for email, banking and work accounts, and increasingly stores passkeys and the codes used for two-factor authentication. If an attacker obtained a copy of encrypted vault data, the strength of the master password would determine how hard it is to crack. That is why changing the master password first, and then changing the most important stored passwords, is the usual response in these situations.

Users who have mSecure data can take a few sensible steps while waiting for more information. Change the master password to a long, unique one. Then change passwords for the most sensitive accounts first, such as email, banking and any account that can be used to reset others. Re-enroll two-factor authentication where the codes were stored in the app, replace passkeys that were saved there, and watch for phishing emails that claim to come from mSecure, since attackers often exploit news of a breach.

Many questions remain open. It is not clear how many customers are affected, whether the incident involved stolen data or only unauthorized access attempts, or whether the company will publish a fuller explanation. Customers are likely to look for those details before deciding whether to keep using the service or switch to another password manager.

items.title: Netflix’s new AI Discover tab helps you find something to watch based on your mood
items.summary: Netflix has begun testing "AI Discover," a new tab in its TV app that suggests shows and movies based on what you feel like watching, and it plans to expand the experiment to more viewers in the coming weeks.
items.articleBody:
Netflix has started rolling out "AI Discover," a new tab in its TV app that uses artificial intelligence to help subscribers decide what to watch. The company announced the feature on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and described it as a place to try out new ways of finding content. The first experiment inside the tab recommends titles based on what a viewer is in the mood for.

Instead of a standard row of thumbnails, the tab offers a set of curated themes that can include clips from shows and movies. Viewers can pick a theme that matches their mood, their viewing preferences, how much time they have, or what is new and trending. Examples reported by the press include themes such as "Scare Me" and "Quick Watches." If none of the options appeals, a "Something Different" choice brings up a new set of themes. Users who have access will see a Discover button with a red gem icon and a "New" label in the top navigation bar.

Netflix says the feature runs on a new intelligence layer that responds to what users tell it in real time and keeps learning. Some coverage notes that, because the recommendations are generated live, even Netflix could not predict exactly what would appear on screen during a demonstration. The company has also called the tab a "test kitchen," a space for trying early-stage discovery ideas and seeing which ones people actually use.

The rollout is limited for now. AI Discover is starting in the United States for English-language profiles on supported TVs, and it is reaching a small group of members first. Netflix says it plans to bring the tab to additional users in the coming weeks.

The move reflects a broader effort to make the service's large catalog easier to navigate. Netflix has long relied on recommendations built from viewing history, Thumbs Up ratings and items added to My List. The company says AI Discover joins those tools as a new way to explore, not a replacement. The change also suggests a shift away from endless scrolling and toward a more conversational, personalized approach to choosing what to watch.

Some questions remain open. Netflix has not shared data showing that mood-based browsing leads to better viewing satisfaction, and it is not yet clear how well it will work in different situations, such as a household sharing one profile. It is also unclear which features will be added to the tab next, or whether it will reach every subscriber and device. Those answers are likely to emerge as more viewers try it over the coming weeks.

items.title: Today’s Android app deals and freebies: 20 Minutes Till Dawn, Never Grave, Rush Rally 3, more

A new batch of Google Play discounts appeared on November 3, 2026, covering paid Android games and apps that were marked down or made free for a limited time. The deals were collected by 9to5Toys, which noted that the offer window has since closed. Because Play Store prices can change without notice, anyone interested should check the current price on the app's store page before buying.

The Reigns series, This War of Mine and Shotgun King were discounted as well, with This War of Mine falling to $2 from a regular price of $13.

These included The Room Stalker, Hello Human: AI Puzzle Game, Dungeon Princess 2, Live or Die: Survival Pro, Mekaro: Open World Mech RPG, AimSize: Object Size Measure, SciFi Survivor Premium and the two King of Defense Premium games. Their regular prices ranged from a few cents to a few dollars, and Mekaro and Space Shooter: Galaxy Attack had regular prices of $7 and $22 respectively, which makes the free offers more notable.

The roundup also referred readers to other hardware deals that were running at the time, including an all-time low on the new Google Home Speaker during an early Black Friday sale, as well as price cuts on Pixel 11 phones and a first deal on Amazon's new Alexa Android tablet.

A few cautions apply. Price drops on Google Play usually last only a short time, and developers can end them early or extend them. Regional pricing also varies, so the amounts quoted here are U.S. dollar prices and may differ in other countries. Free-for-a-limited-time apps typically stay in a user's library after being claimed, but the terms depend on the developer, so it is worth reading the store listing first. As Black Friday approaches, more app and hardware discounts are likely to appear.

items.title: Apple’s latest watchOS beta includes its new always-on Audio Intelligence features
items.summary: Apple has released a watchOS 27.3 developer beta that lets developers and early testers try Siri Recap and Live Rewind, two opt-in Apple Watch features that use the microphone to help people remember conversations.
items.articleBody:
Apple has started letting early testers try its new Audio Intelligence features on the Apple Watch. The two additions, Siri Recap and Live Rewind, are included in the watchOS 27.3 developer beta that began rolling out this week. Both features allow Siri to use the watch's microphone to help wearers remember what was said around them, which is why they have drawn attention from privacy observers as well as Apple fans.

Siri Recap is designed to summarize conversations so that users can refresh their memory later. It uses what Apple and press coverage describe as ambient listening. The feature is opt-in and can be limited by schedule, for example by time of day or by location, and it can be switched on or off from Control Center once it has been enabled.

Live Rewind has a narrower purpose. It works from a short rolling buffer of roughly 15 seconds of audio that is constantly overwritten. When the wearer double-presses the Digital Crown, the watch turns those last few seconds of speech into text on the screen. Apple suggests uses such as catching a detail that someone mentioned quickly. Because the watch's chip does not handle the transcription on its own, the feature relies on the paired iPhone and does not work when the phone is out of range.

Apple says both features are opt-in and that raw audio is not recorded or made available to apps or to Apple. Reporting on the beta says that audio is processed and then discarded, and that Live Rewind plays a chime and shows a visual alert when it is used, so people nearby have some indication. Even so, critics point out that bystanders have not agreed to be listened to, and that an alert after the fact may not help someone who has just spoken.

The features are tied to the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, which Apple introduced in September alongside the broader Audio Intelligence suite. That suite also includes Sound Recognition and music recognition with Shazam. Developer betas are intended for testing, so the behavior, wording and options of these features could change before a public release.

What happens next is still uncertain. Apple has not said when watchOS 27.3 will reach all users, and it remains to be seen how many people will turn on features that depend on an always-ready microphone. How the beta performs in real conversations, and whether Apple adjusts its privacy controls in response to feedback, will probably shape how widely the tools are accepted.

items.title: OpenAI says ChatGPT is catching up to Google in search
items.summary: OpenAI says the number of search-style queries handled by ChatGPT has grown to roughly one-fifth of Google's volume. The figure is the company's own claim and has not been independently verified.
items.articleBody:
OpenAI says ChatGPT is closing in on Google when it comes to search. Adam Fry, the company's consumer product lead for ChatGPT, said the volume of search-like queries on ChatGPT is now roughly one-fifth of Google's. He made the remark in an interview with Alex Kantrowitz of Big Technology at an OpenAI-hosted dinner in New York on Monday, November 2, 2026, and the comment was widely reported over the following days.

Fry defined a search broadly, describing it as any time a user asks a question and the system goes out to search the web. According to coverage of the interview, the comparison counts only prompts that trigger a web search, not every conversation people have with the chatbot. Fry also pointed out that ChatGPT used to rely only on its training data, which made it less useful for current information. Now that it can reach the live web, he said, many interactions resemble the lookups people once did on a search engine.

The same interview contained other growth figures. Fry said ChatGPT's weekly active users rose from about 1 billion to roughly 1.2 billion in just two months, an increase of around 200 million. He also said that about 250 million people now use ChatGPT's voice features each week. "The growth is just going big," he said.

Context matters when reading the 20 percent figure. It comes from OpenAI itself, and the company has not published the data or method behind it. It also has not said what number it used for Google's search volume. Because of that, the claim is difficult to verify independently, and it should not be read as ChatGPT having a 20 percent share of the search market. It is a comparison of two volumes using OpenAI's own definition of a search. Google, for its part, has said its search volume is at an all-time high, so the numbers do not necessarily mean that ChatGPT is taking queries away from Google.

The timing is worth noting. Several reports point out that OpenAI is reportedly exploring a public listing, and that the company is also looking at ads and new interface features for ChatGPT. Strong usage numbers are useful for a company that wants to show investors and advertisers that its product is becoming a mainstream way to find information.

For publishers and marketers, the claim adds to an ongoing shift. If more people ask a chatbot instead of typing a query into a search engine, traffic patterns change, and websites and brands may need to think about how they appear in AI-generated answers as well as in traditional results.

Many questions remain unanswered. It is unclear how OpenAI measures a search-like query, how that compares with Google's own counting, and whether the growth will continue at the same pace. Independent data from outside analysts would help show how much of this activity is really replacing traditional search.

items.title: Chainstack Reports Production Systems Breach Exposing Customer Data and Password Hashes
items.summary: Blockchain infrastructure provider Chainstack says an outside attacker got into part of its systems through a third-party component and reached a database holding customer account details, including password hashes. The company says the access has been cut off and is asking customers to take protective steps.
items.articleBody:
Chainstack, a company that provides blockchain node and infrastructure services, has disclosed a security breach that exposed some customer account information. According to the company, an external attacker gained unauthorized access to part of its infrastructure through a third-party component, then moved from a development environment into production systems.

Reports based on Chainstack's disclosure place the intrusion between October 26 and October 31, 2026. The attacker is said to have entered a development environment on October 26, reached production on October 29, and was cut off on October 31. Chainstack says it detected the intrusion, closed the access paths and is now hardening its systems. A later update said the incident had been contained and that customer-facing services kept running normally throughout.

The attacker accessed a database that holds customer account information. The data that may have been exposed includes organization names, account holder names, the email addresses of organization members, and password hashes. Chainstack says it does not store full payment card numbers or security codes, so that information was not affected. The company also says customer nodes, its console and its API were not modified.

The company has also pointed to a second area of concern. The attacker had access to systems that hold node credentials. Chainstack says it has no evidence those credentials were read, but it is treating them as exposed and has asked customers to rotate them. This is a cautious approach, since credentials that could have been seen are safest when replaced.

Some reports link the attack to an AI-driven campaign. The Block reported that the attacker obtained machine credentials that reached production and used the ARTEX AI agent framework to carry out the breach, and other security outlets note that several companies have disclosed similar incidents around the same time. Those details come from secondary reporting on the incident, so readers should rely on Chainstack's own notice for what is confirmed.

For customers, the main risks come from the password hashes. A hash is not a plain-text password, but weak or reused passwords can sometimes be cracked, and password reuse can then let attackers try the same credentials on other services. Customers should change their Chainstack password, change it anywhere else it was reused, rotate node credentials and API keys, turn on multi-factor authentication where possible, and watch for phishing messages that claim to come from Chainstack.

The incident also shows how a weakness in a third-party tool can give attackers a path from a development environment into production. Organizations are advised to review which components connect those environments and to make sure a compromised development tool cannot reach production data or secrets.

Open questions remain. Chainstack has not said how many customers were affected, which third-party component was involved, or whether any data was actually copied out. The company's updates are likely to clarify those points as its investigation continues.

items.title: ‘Cyclon’ uses an old Google Pixel to let AI do literally everything for you – who wants this?
items.summary: Y Combinator-backed startup Cyclon is taking pre-orders for an AI-first phone that operates your existing apps for you. Early buyers get a repurposed Google Pixel 8a running its software first, while the company's own $699 phone is expected in 2027.
items.articleBody:
A startup called Cyclon is pitching a different kind of smartphone, one where an AI assistant does most of the tapping, typing and replying on your behalf. The company, which came out of Y Combinator's F26 batch, has opened pre-orders for what it describes as an AI phone that gets things done across the apps people already use. Its stated ambition is to eventually replace the iPhone.

The idea works through a chatbot-style interface. Instead of opening apps one by one, users tell the system what they want. Cyclon says the software can manage notifications, send messages, generate responses for the user, order things through existing apps, and even build small apps on demand, such as a language-learning app made for a specific trip. The company says it works with apps people already have installed, without requiring those apps to add special integrations.

To get the software into people's hands sooner, Cyclon is starting with recycled hardware. A working prototype runs on Google Pixel 8a phones. Eligible first-batch buyers in the United States who place a pre-order are promised a Pixel 8a prototype running Cyclon OS within 30 days, at no extra cost. During this early-access period, the company says no subscription is required and AI usage is included. Reports say that it ships only within the U.S., although pre-orders can be placed from anywhere.

The pre-order itself is a $199 deposit, which the company describes as fully refundable. It reserves a later device, the Cyclon Phone, which is the company's own hardware and is expected in the second quarter of 2027. The estimated final price is $699. The Pixel prototype is meant as a stand-in, not as the finished product, and the company has not yet said where the Cyclon Phone will ship.

Not everyone is convinced. A 9to5Google commentary questioned who actually wants a phone that sends everything through a chatbot and writes replies in the user's name. The concern is less about convenience than about control, because letting software handle messages and purchases means trusting it with sensitive tasks and personal data. Other analysts note that the claim of doing "everything" has not been tested by independent reviewers, and that it is unclear which tasks users will actually want to hand over.

The project also invites comparison with earlier AI gadgets that promised to replace the smartphone and struggled to deliver, such as the Humane AI Pin. Cyclon's approach is different in one way, since it builds on a familiar phone and the apps people already use instead of asking them to adopt a new type of device.

Many details are still unknown, including which AI models power the system, how reliably it handles the quirks of different apps, how it protects user data when it acts inside banking, messaging or shopping apps, and what ongoing costs will look like once early access ends. For now, Cyclon is best seen as an early experiment, and the real test will come when buyers start using it in daily life.

items.title: SUSE lays off 1 in 10 workers – citing AI and automation
items.summary: Linux and open-source software company SUSE is cutting about 10% of its global workforce, roughly 190 of its 1,900 employees. CEO Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen blamed automation and AI for changing how software companies operate.
items.articleBody:
SUSE, the German enterprise Linux and open-source software company, is laying off about 10 percent of its global workforce. Chief executive Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen announced the cuts in an internal memo to staff on Monday, November 2, 2026. With roughly 1,900 employees, the reduction amounts to about 190 jobs.

In the memo, van Leeuwen said automation and AI are changing how software companies work. According to reports, he described the shift as reducing the need for some roles and allowing the company to operate with less overhead and a flatter structure. The cuts were described as a painful decision.

The timeline is short. Affected employees were due to be notified by November 4, with one-to-one meetings starting the week after. Reports say the company moved ahead with layoffs after too few employees took up an earlier offer of voluntary exits.

The announcement stands out because it names AI directly as the reason. Several outlets have counted a number of recent job cuts in the technology sector, and most of those they reviewed referred to AI in an employer's own documents or in an executive's comments. Website builder Squarespace also announced layoffs this week, but reports suggest its explicit links to AI have been less consistent. SUSE's explanation is therefore one of the clearer examples of a company tying cuts to AI.

There are also complicating details. SUSE itself sells software and tools that help customers automate IT work, so it is reorganizing its own workforce around the same trend it promotes to clients. The company has not published productivity data or estimated how many roles AI could take over. In addition, SUSE is owned by the investment firm EQT, and Reuters reported in March that EQT was considering selling it, which means cost pressure and ownership plans may also play a role in the decision.

Staff in Prague have formed a union, the SUSE Workers Union, under the Czech ICT Union, with AI use and pay among the topics raised. One report noted that no link has been shown between the layoffs or exit offers and the union's formation.

The cuts matter for people inside the open-source community as well as for SUSE's customers. SUSE is a major vendor of Linux and Kubernetes-related products, and a smaller workforce could affect support, development and the pace of new releases, although the company has not said which teams are affected.

Key questions remain unanswered. SUSE has not said which roles or regions will lose the most jobs, how much it expects to save, or how AI tools will replace the work that departing employees did. How the company explains those details in the coming weeks will help show whether AI is the main cause of the cuts or one of several factors.

items.title: Google’s Stadia Controller dream lives on in the $50 Xbox Nano Controller
items.summary: Microsoft's new $50 Xbox Nano Controller includes a "Cloud Connect" feature that links it directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming over Wi-Fi, an approach first popularized by Google's Stadia Controller. The feature is still in preview.
items.articleBody:
Microsoft's new Xbox Nano Controller has a feature that will be familiar to anyone who remembers Google's Stadia. Alongside its small size, the $49.99 gamepad can connect straight to Xbox Cloud Gaming over Wi-Fi, an idea the Stadia Controller introduced years ago. The Nano went on sale on November 4, 2026, after Microsoft announced it in mid-October.

The controller itself is a pocket-sized version of the standard Xbox Wireless Controller. It weighs about 3.5 ounces, has a built-in rechargeable battery, and works with consoles, PCs, mobile devices and some TVs. Microsoft also priced it at €49.99 in Europe and £44.99 in the United Kingdom. It uses Xbox Wireless and Bluetooth for local connections.

The less obvious feature is called Cloud Connect. Microsoft describes it as pairing the Nano over Wi-Fi to give a fast and responsive Xbox Cloud Gaming experience. With a normal controller, inputs usually travel to a phone, TV or PC over Bluetooth and are then relayed to the cloud. With a direct Wi-Fi link, the controller can talk to Microsoft's servers on its own, which removes a step and should reduce input lag. That is the same approach Google took with the Stadia Controller, which connected directly to Google's cloud infrastructure.

The feature is not fully available to everyone yet. Reports say it is in beta, and that it first appeared on Microsoft's newer Xbox Cloud Gaming website. Setup involves pairing the controller over Wi-Fi, and after that, signing in to a supported cloud session with the same Xbox account used for setup makes the controller connect on its own. Coverage by Notebookcheck says users have to be enrolled in the Xbox Insider program to set it up through the PC app, and Engadget reports that it is limited to users in the United States and works only on smart TVs and the web for now. Windows Central said at launch that the feature was not yet active.

Microsoft is also testing another cloud-related idea, which lets people use a smartphone as a controller for Xbox Cloud Gaming on supported smart TVs. Taken together, the two tests suggest Microsoft wants cloud gaming to feel less dependent on a console or a PC, and cheaper to get started with.

The comparison with Stadia is more of a symbolic nod than a sign of a comeback. Google's service has been shut down for years, but its controller showed that a direct connection can improve responsiveness. Microsoft now has a larger cloud library and an existing subscriber base to build on.

Several questions remain open. Microsoft has not said when Cloud Connect will leave beta, when it will reach more countries, or whether it will ever work with consoles instead of only with cloud gaming. It also remains to be seen how big the latency improvement is in everyday use, because that depends on a player's home Wi-Fi and internet connection. Independent reviews should give a clearer picture once the feature is available to more people.

items.title: How to make your older Android phones last longer
items.summary: An older Android phone can keep working well for years with a few habits: protecting the battery, freeing up storage, keeping software updated, and shielding the device from physical damage.
items.articleBody:
Many Android phones are replaced long before they stop working. Slower performance, shorter battery life and a worn-looking body often push people to upgrade, yet most of those problems can be reduced with a few simple habits. These steps can help an older phone last longer and save money.

Start with the battery, because it is usually the first part to wear out. Lithium-ion batteries age fastest when they are kept at very high or very low charge and when they get hot. Try to keep the charge roughly between 20 and 80 percent when possible, avoid leaving the phone in a hot car or in direct sun, and take off thick cases while charging if the phone gets warm. Many Android phones include an adaptive or limited charging setting that slows charging overnight or stops at a set level, which can reduce wear. If the battery has already faded badly, replacing it at a reputable repair shop is often much cheaper than buying a new phone.

Next, free up storage. A phone that is almost full tends to slow down because it has little room to work with. Delete apps you no longer use, clear app caches, move photos and videos to cloud storage or a computer, and remove large downloaded files. Aim to leave at least 10 to 15 percent of the storage free. Restarting the phone every few days also clears temporary processes and can help with sluggish behavior.

Keep the software up to date for as long as your phone is supported. Updates include security patches and bug fixes, and they matter more than new features. When a phone no longer receives official updates, be more careful, because it becomes easier to attack. Install apps only from trusted sources such as the Google Play Store, review the permissions each app asks for, and uninstall anything that seems suspicious. Using lighter versions of heavy apps, such as the "Lite" editions that some services offer, can also make an older phone feel faster.

Reduce background activity. Open the battery and app settings and look for apps that use a lot of power or run constantly in the background. Limit their background use, turn off unneeded notifications, and disable animations or lower the screen refresh rate if your phone allows it. Lower screen brightness and a shorter screen timeout also help, since the display is one of the biggest power drains.

Protect the hardware. A good case and a tempered glass screen protector cost little and can prevent expensive damage. Keep charging ports clean, since lint and dust can cause loose connections, and use a quality charger and cable from a known brand. Cheap, unbranded chargers can deliver unstable power and harm the battery over time. Avoid exposing the phone to water, even if it has a water-resistance rating, because seals weaken as the phone ages.

Finally, consider a fresh start. If the phone has become slow despite these steps, back up your data and perform a factory reset. This removes years of accumulated files, settings and leftover app data. Set the phone up again and install only the apps you actually use. If the phone is still struggling, a lighter launcher or a custom ROM from a trusted community project may extend its life, although that route carries some risk and may void the warranty.

None of these steps will make an old phone like new, and hardware eventually reaches its limits. But taking care of the battery, storage, software and body can add a year or more of useful life, and that is good for your budget and for the environment.

items.title: CrowdStrike to shell out nearly $500M for 2 AI security startups as the market for securing agents takes off
items.summary: CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire two AI security startups, Fiddler AI and Dreadnode, in deals reportedly worth about $495 million combined. The purchases add tools for monitoring AI agents and for testing them against attacks before they go live.
items.articleBody:
CrowdStrike has announced that it will buy two startups focused on securing AI agents, Fiddler AI and Dreadnode. The Wall Street Journal, which reported the deals ahead of the official announcements on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, said CrowdStrike is paying around $400 million for Fiddler and about $95 million for Dreadnode, a combined total of roughly $495 million. The report described the deals as mostly in cash, and CrowdStrike itself has not confirmed the prices.

Fiddler AI, founded in 2018 and based in Palo Alto, California, makes observability software that helps companies watch what AI agents are doing inside their networks. CrowdStrike plans to fold the technology into its Falcon platform as a new product called Falcon Observe. The tool is meant to help customers test agents before they are deployed, trace the reasoning and tool calls behind an agent's actions, and watch for problems in production, such as behavioral drift and made-up answers. Fiddler has raised about $100 million in total funding, according to SecurityWeek.

Dreadnode, founded in 2023, focuses on a different part of the problem. Its software automates security testing for AI models, applications and agents, so that flaws can be found before the systems go live. Users can describe in plain language what they want to test, and the platform runs a large library of known attack methods, including jailbreaks, prompt injection and multi-step attacks aimed at agents. It also checks the MCP servers that agents rely on and ranks its findings by severity. The startup has raised about $14 million. CrowdStrike plans to feed Dreadnode's results into its Falcon Guardian product, which maps the AI agents in a company's environment and makes security recommendations.

The timing reflects how quickly companies are putting AI agents to work. Agents can take actions on their own, such as calling tools and accessing data, which creates new risks that traditional security products were not designed to handle. Fiddler's chief executive, Krishna Gade, said that as AI security and observability come together, companies need to understand what their agents do, step in when they go off course, and explain why.

CrowdStrike expects the Fiddler deal to close in the fourth quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, subject to closing conditions, and Falcon Observe is scheduled to launch in that same period. Dreadnode's team, led by CEO Brad Palm, will join CrowdStrike's Cyber Superintelligence Lab, and testing capabilities based on its technology are also expected to be generally available in that quarter. The acquisitions follow CrowdStrike's earlier agreement, in September 2025, to buy AI security company Pangea.

Several details are still unclear. CrowdStrike has not officially confirmed the price of each deal, and it has not said how the products will be priced for customers or how many of the startups' existing customers will stay. It also remains to be seen whether adding these tools to a large security platform will make them more useful than standalone products, or whether other security vendors will respond with deals of their own.

items.title: HomeView with an arm? Apple reportedly plans $1,000 swiveling smart panel
items.summary: Apple is reportedly developing a higher-end HomeView with a 9-inch screen on a motorized arm that turns the display toward whoever is speaking. Reports say it could cost about $1,000 and arrive in 2027 or 2028, but Apple has announced nothing.
items.articleBody:
Apple is reportedly working on a premium version of its HomeView smart display that adds a robotic arm. According to a report from The Information, published in early November 2026, the device could be sold as the "HomeView Ultra" and is internally codenamed J595. Apple has not announced the product or confirmed any name, price or release date.

The device is said to have a roughly 9-inch touchscreen mounted on a swiveling arm. Descriptions in the coverage compare its design to the Pixar lamp and to the old iMac G4. That would make it larger than the HomeView that Apple recently launched, which has a 7-inch display on a hinge that can only be tilted by hand. The standard model costs $299.

The arm is the main difference. Reports say it can rotate the screen a full 360 degrees, and that cameras, sensors and voice recognition would let it face the person who is speaking. One example given is a FaceTime call in which the display follows someone as they move around the kitchen. Another reported idea is that the device could switch on a light when someone enters the room. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman had earlier reported on the same product, a higher-end HomeView with a robotic arm, and its codename.

Price and timing are less certain. The target price is reported to be around $1,000 in the United States, more than three times the cost of the current model. Some reports say price increases for memory and other components are part of the reason. Apple is said to be aiming for a 2027 launch, but several outlets note that the release could slip to 2028. Some coverage says the hardware has been ready for about two years, and that software problems are what is holding it back.

That software point matters. A display that moves and reacts to people in a room puts a lot of pressure on the assistant behind it. Commentators say that for a $1,000 product to succeed, Apple's voice assistant and AI features need to be reliable, because every weakness would be more noticeable on a device that behaves like a participant in the conversation.

The product also has a clear predecessor in the market. Amazon's Echo Show 10 had a screen that rotated to follow users, but it was later discontinued, which raises the question of whether a moving smart display can find a large audience. Apple would need to show that the arm solves a real problem and not just adds a novelty.

Many questions remain. Apple has not confirmed any of the reported specifications, and it is unclear whether the device would be sold outside the United States, what it would be called, or how much of its functionality would depend on new AI features. As with any report about unreleased hardware, plans can change before a product reaches stores.
